documents.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is one of the most common oral malignancies. Due to insidious early symptoms, high invasiveness, and frequent cervical lymph node metastasis, patient survival remains poor. Recent studies demonstrate significant associations between oral dysbiosis and OSCC. To address limited early screening and suboptimal survival rates, this review systematically summarizes OSCC microbiome research and disease risk assessment applications. Studies reveal marked oral dysbiosis in patients with OSCC, characterized by enrichment of Fusobacterium and Porphyromonas , reduced Neisseria abundance, and altered community stability. These promote tumorigenesis through chronic pro-inflammatory signaling, the production of carcinogenic metabolites, and direct oncogenic pathway interference. Consequently, the oral microbiome offers non-invasive, sensitive biomarkers for early detection. We identify and distinguish four categories of predictive models in the current literature: (1) detection/discrimination of prevalent OSCC, (2) prediction of malignant transformation from oral potentially malignant disorders, (3) prediction of recurrence or metastasis after treatment, and (4) prognostic models for survival prediction. Existing databases include comprehensive and OSCC-specific collections with multi-omics integration. Risk assessment models encompass traditional statistics, machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal fusion, and have shown promising performance in retrospective cohorts. However, standardized databases are lacking, and existing models face confounding interference, limited generalizability, and insufficient interpretability. Furthermore, current predictive models are predominantly based on 16S rRNA sequencing (bacteriome-centric), whereas comprehensive risk assessment requires integrating interkingdom entities, including fungi, viruses, and archaea, through metagenomic and virome profiling. Critically, the distinction between promising retrospective discrimination and validated prospective clinical utility remains a major translational barrier. Future directions include developing standardized longitudinal databases, integrating multi-omics, using explainable artificial intelligence, and conducting prospective validation studies to achieve personalized precision treatment.

Hierarchical task knowledge enables efficient problem solving by allowing previously acquired skills to be reused across tasks and problem instances. In this paper, we investigate curriculum-guided acquisition of hierarchical task knowledge in an HTN learning framework. We compare three approaches: online learning during problem solving, human-designed curricula, and an automated curriculum generation procedure that derives learning experiences from verified LLM-generated solution traces. The proposed procedure solves small training problems with an LLM, extracts task accomplishment information, and transforms it into ordered sequences of state-task learning problems for HTN method acquisition. We evaluate the three approaches across multiple planning domains. The results demonstrate that automatically generated curricula recover much of the benefit of expert-designed curricula while substantially reducing the token cost of online hierarchical knowledge acquisition.

Objectives: This paper examines a central tension within Industry 4.0. Digitalisation can improve efficiency, monitoring capacity and decision making, but it also creates vulnerabilities linked to digital system failures, cyber incidents and algorithmic bias. The study analyses how these risks condition sustainable and resilient digital transformation in industrial environments and why they are relevant to smart cities. Prior work: The paper builds on research on Industry 4.0, digital transformation and productivity, together with studies on cyber physical systems, smart city security, Internet of Things (IoT) vulnerabilities, artificial intelligence (AI) enabled cyber defence and algorithmic governance. It connects these strands to move beyond technical performance and cybersecurity alone. Approach: The study follows a conceptual and analytical approach, supported by selected secondary evidence from Spain and the European context. Spain provides a contextual empirical anchor for illustrating the operational and social relevance of cyber risk, while the European framework supports the analysis of cybersecurity, algorithmic transparency, human oversight and AI governance. Results: The analysis shows that Industry 4.0 should not be assessed only through automation, efficiency or productivity gains. Its sustainability also depends on resilient digital infrastructures and on the governance conditions under which algorithmic systems are deployed. Under opacity, scale and limited accountability, such systems may amplify hidden biases and generate persistent harms in workforce management, supplier selection and investment allocation. Implications: The findings are relevant for researchers, policy makers and practitioners involved in smart industry and smart city strategies, as they stress the need to align innovation with resilience, accountability and organisational trust. Value: The paper contributes an integrated framework linking cyber resilience, algorithmic governance and social sustainability, showing that sustainable digital transformation requires both resilient infrastructures and accountable automated decisions.

documents.abstract: Smart cities use integrated Internet of Things (IoT) devices, cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance efficiency in transportation, energy, health care, waste management and administration. Nevertheless, hyper-connectivity poses extremely complicated issues, in particular, cybersecurity, privacy, and trust. Unauthorized access to IoT device(s) and massive data breaches, plus the abuse of surveillance systems and adversarial manipulating AI systems, all jeopardize urban safety and erode citizen trust. The chapter is an examination of the relationship between cybersecurity, privacy, and trust in the smart city ecosystem based on both a technical and social level. Examining some of the existing vulnerabilities of certain IoT networks, we overview a list of threats, such as data leakage, identity spoofing, and misinformation. Lastly, we speak about the ways of enhancing resilience. We describe emerging solutions to some of those problems, including blockchain-based identity management, privacy-preserving analytics, federated learning, and Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) and analyze their potential for trust enhancing effect(s). As demonstrated in our case study on the evaluation based on simulations, the framework reduces the propagation and distribution of ransomware by more than 86 percent, downtime caused by denial-of-service attacks is decreased 87 percent, and the probability of data leakage is reduced by more than 92 percent. It accomplishes this without impacting predictive accuracy and performance significantly. We propose a proposal to develop a secure and privacy-conscious and reliable smart city ecosystem by integrating both technological means of protection and dedicating ourselves to citizen-driven governance.

Modern digital life requires individuals to navigate an expansive and fragmented cyber landscape composed of heterogeneous online accounts, cloud services, interconnected mobile endpoints, and smart IoT devices. Despite escalating threats—including automated credential stuffing, sophisticated phishing campaigns, zero-day endpoint vulnerabilities, and passive digital footprint accumulation—contemporary personal cybersecurity relies predominantly on fragmented, reactive utility tools such as isolated password vaults, signature-based desktop antivirus engines, and sporadic breach lookup portals. These disconnected point solutions lack holistic contextual awareness and fail to furnish unified visibility into an individual's compounding cyber exposure. In this research, we propose CyberTwin: a unified, intelligent digital twin framework engineered specifically for personal cyber safety. CyberTwin synthesizes continuous asset telemetry, multi-vector threat detection, and explainable behavioral nudges to construct a synchronized, virtual representation of a user's digital ecosystem. Architected with a modular, high-concurrency web technology stack comprising a React.js and Tailwind CSS user interface, an asynchronous Python FastAPI backend, Pydantic v2 data validation schemas, SQLAlchemy ORM, and a centralized MySQL persistence layer, the platform incorporates a two-tier cascaded threat engine fusing a 1D-CNN+Bi-GRU deep neural network with large language model (LLM) contextual reasoning, a real-time lexical URL analyzer, and an Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)-grounded personal risk diagnostic model. Security is enforced through JSON Web Token (JWT) role authorization, salted bcrypt hashing, and TLS communication. Benchmarked across a comprehensive empirical testbed of 500 ground-truth threat vectors (Nazario, PhishTank, Enron) and simulated identity topologies, CyberTwin demonstrated a 68% acceleration in threat detection cycle times, sub-125 ms API service response latency, and a 91.2% overall satisfaction rating in user evaluations.

ABSTRACT Simulating human mobility is crucial for urban planning, environmental exposure assessment, and social behavior studies. However, existing methods often rely on rules and assumptions, making it difficult to provide robust results and explicit decision‐making processes when generating plausible daily activity trajectories from sparse location records such as check‐ins. To bridge these gaps, we propose a large language model (LLM)‐based agent framework that innovatively incorporates the Chain‐of‐Thought (CoT) approach and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) mechanisms, namely Daily mobility LLM (DaiLLM). This framework consists of three modules: the Profiler derives user characteristics from historical trajectory data; the Generator simulates movement through the CoT process, which integrates constraints from Profiler outputs; and the Discriminator employs RLAIF to evaluate the similarity between generated results and real data, providing feedback to optimize the results. Experiments demonstrate that: (1) our method improves accuracy by 34.2% compared to traditional approaches in daily activity trajectory generation; (2) the CoT approach enhances activity logic and results in a 26.1% increase through task decomposition and constraint integration; (3) the RLAIF mechanism explicitly provides an optimization process through Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) analysis; and (4) our method excels in transfer learning and long‐term generation across different city contexts. This study provides a robust, transparent, and cost‐effective solution for plausible daily activity trajectory generation from sparse check‐in data, which will establish a new paradigm for mobility behavior analysis in data‐scarce scenarios.

Abstract Artificial intelligence is routinely described as a knowledge technology. This paper argues that the description misplaces a boundary Hayek drew in 1945, between “scientific knowledge”—codifiable, statistical, articulable—and “knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place.” Kiesling (2015) reconstructs part of the latter as the contextual knowledge problem: knowledge that does not exist outside the interaction producing it, as against the complexity problem of aggregating knowledge that exists dispersed but can in principle be codified. The reconstruction is interpretive and identifies a generative subset of Hayek’s category rather than its whole content; much of the remainder is knowledge agents already possess, and AI dissolves a good deal of it. The argument is not that machine systems cannot discover novel alternatives, nor that their search spaces are closed; both are conceded. It is that discovering means does not originate the ultimate ends by reference to which alternatives acquire economic significance, and that current systems receive those ends rather than constituting them. Under a Misesian account of evaluative agency—a premise the paper declares rather than derives—better aggregation, prediction and optimisation therefore cannot by themselves resolve the generative subset, so neither Polanyian tacit knowledge in large language models nor microstructure price discovery by high-frequency traders reaches it. The taxonomy is applied at three levels—the data pipeline, the tacit-knowledge debate, and the institutional conditions of price generation—as three applications of one classification rather than three independent demonstrations. Its products are a set of operational tests, none of which has been run and which are here read against a published Q-learning pricing architecture, and a criterion distinguishing context-preserving from context-suppressing deployment at the level of the market.

Drilling organizations require performance information that identifies weakened controls and supports effective corrective action. This paper develops a conceptual framework for data driven health, safety and environmental monitoring in Saudi oil and gas drilling operations. A purposive integrative review combines peer reviewed leading indicator research with primary technical guidance and descriptive corporate disclosures. It distinguishes occupational safety, occupational health, environmental management and process safety, arguing that aggregate injury indicators cannot represent every consequential exposure. The proposed framework connects validated reporting, risk triage, cause analysis, accountable intervention and independent effectiveness verification. Three analytical tables specify evidence boundaries, indicator definitions and a corrective action workflow. A graph illustrates selected published corporate measures without attributing them to drilling sites. The analysis identifies denominator consistency, contractor interfaces, reporting protection and verification quality as conditions for useful monitoring. Three propositions support future field testing. No original rig observations or causal estimates are claimed. The framework offers a practical research agenda for operational capability and responsible industrial development associated with Vision 2030.

In high-stakes domains such as finance, critical information evolves through multi-party interaction. Recovering these changes and their sources is fundamental to reliable speech understanding. Existing speech benchmarks focus on transcription, local understanding, and turn-level state prediction, leaving joint decision evolution across speakers insufficiently evaluated. We introduce DecisionTraceBench, a speech state-tracking benchmark for Decision-Critical Information State Tracking (DCIST). It jointly evaluates decision event sequences, speaker attribution, scope, and temporal evidence, using trajectory-level F1 to measure complete event-chain recovery. Our dataset comprises Chinese financial dialogues involving two to four speakers, with 100.39 hours of synthetic audio and 8.61 hours of human-performed recordings. On a fixed cohort of human-performed recordings, five cascaded systems and two direct-audio models achieve DCIST scores of 5.73% to 21.35%. Ablations with speaker-labeled reference scripts and no temporal localization requirements yield a maximum score of only 38.72%. Audio perturbation experiments further show that overall transcription error rates do not adequately reflect complete trajectory recovery. These findings reveal limitations in jointly understanding information provenance and state evolution, providing a benchmark for evaluating decision-process understanding and decision traceability in high-stakes speech applications.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly promoted as decolonial tools for preserving Indigenous languages, yet whether such methods can be decolonial remains contested. This paper conceptualizes that debate through the distinction between functional and critical interculturality, separating recognition of cultural difference from the redistribution of power over knowledge production. Rather than resolving this distinction from literature alone, we investigate how it is translated into the perspectives of an Indigenous community itself, drawing on twelve interviews with Zapotec speakers in Oaxaca, Mexico, about AI and LLM-based tools for language preservation. We find that participants’ own accounts divide along these same lines: some value the technical recognition LLMs offer their language, while a majority articulate a critical position, arguing that these technologies are designed within and for the ideological frameworks of culturally dominant countries and that the resources they require make independent community development virtually impossible. Building on this division, we propose critical interculturality of data as an analytical framework that shifts attention from whether Indigenous languages are represented in digital and computational methods to who controls the terms of that representation, pointing to community-led alternatives practiced beyond AI.

documents.abstract: The Jet Boring System (JBS) is a proprietary technology developed by Cameco Corporation to extract high-grade uranium ore at the Cigar Lake Mine in Northern Saskatchewan, Canada. The JBS remotely excavates ore using a high-pressure water jet that cuts cavities within an artificially frozen ore body. This study outlines a Deep Learning (DL)-based workflow that formulates the cavity prediction problem as a volumetric binary semantic segmentation task. A preprocessing pipeline assembles drilling and jetting records, cavity scans, and a mine-wide geology block model onto a common voxel grid, where each voxel in the prediction is labelled as consumed or non-consumed during jetting. A three-dimensional U-Net with a backfill residual branch is trained on historical field cavities. The model is benchmarked against a baseline consisting of a cylindrical cavity centered along the pilot hole, with a diameter defined by domain experts. The proposed workflow achieves an IoU of 0.601 $\pm$ 0.088 and an F$_1$-Score of 0.747 $\pm$ 0.077 on a held-out test set, improving on the cylindrical baseline currently used in cavity planning by 22.4% and 14.7%, respectively. An eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) feature attribution approach is applied to identify the most influential input driving the predicted cavity geometry. The accuracy of the proposed model demonstrates its potential to support mine planning.

DELAD provides a forum for addressing technical, legal and ethical issues in sharing disordered speech data and supports secure, responsible archiving. We organise workshops and invite researchers to discuss open-access practices. Suggestions and action points raised by workshop participants are systematically followed up and integrated into the ongoing work. This paper reports on the developments of DELAD which included the new 'Corpora of Disordered Speech' entry in the CLARIN Resource Families, listing 32 datasets, with key metadata and descriptions. The seventh DELAD workshop was held alongside the 21st International Congress of Linguists in Poznań, 2024. The programme covered advances in data sharing infrastructures, metadata design and the balance between transparency and security, with a focus on the potential of large language models in disordered-speech research. Our online survey about data sharing experiences revealed a conflict between the demand for data reuse and the capacity to share. DELAD welcomes collaboration that aligns with its mission.

Objectives: This study examined dental hygiene students' perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted instruction and the factors influencing their satisfaction with such classes. Methods: A self-administered questionnaire was completed by 80 dental hygiene students who participated in an AI-assisted course. The survey evaluated AI usability, the perceived usefulness of learning activities, learning outcomes, and overall class satisfaction. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, and a hierarchical multiple regression analysis. Results: The mean scores for AI usability and perceived usefulness for learning activities were 4.30 and 4.23, respectively. Among the learning outcomes, collaborative competency received the highest mean score of 4.08, followed by academic achievement at 3.91 and learning motivation and self-efficacy at 3.85. The mean class satisfaction score was 3.76. Students who demonstrated higher AI competency, academic achievement, expected course grades, teamwork, and learning participation reported significantly greater AI usability, perceived usefulness of learning activities, learning outcomes, and class satisfaction (p<0.001). The results of the regression analysis showed that learning outcomes (β=0.381, p<0.001) were the most influential factor on class satisfaction, and academic achievement (β=0.289, p<0.001) and AI competency (β=0.193, p=0.013) were also identified as related factors. Conclusions: These findings indicate that dental hygiene students hold positive perceptions of AI-assisted classes. Importantly, learning outcomes emerge as critical determinants of class satisfaction. Therefore, AI-assisted education should extend beyond the mere introduction of AI tools by enhancing AI literacy and integrating AI thoughtfully into instructional design.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in higher education. Yet educators often adopt it more slowly and cautiously than students, and generic guidance rarely translates into changes in teaching or assessment practice. We designed a short, hands-on, pedagogy-first workshop in which life-science educators work with their own course materials, intended to increase confidence in pedagogically informed AI use and prompt concrete changes to course design, teaching and assessment. However, this is an exploratory feasibility and specification report; therefore, the evaluation was not designed to test that intention. Here we describe the design of a transferable three-session FEBS Education and Training Academy module, organised around the PICRAT (Passive-Interactive-Creative/Replace-Amplify-Transform) framework, a four-element prompt structure and studio-style application to participants' own teaching artefacts, and evaluate it using matched pre/post surveys, anonymous after-session feedback and an online follow-up meeting. Thirty-four educators from 14 countries attended; 21 completed the pre-workshop and 13 the post-workshop survey (12 matched). Among the 12 respondents who completed both surveys, the proportion reporting high confidence rose by the same margin, 4 of 12, in each of the five practical domains. Ten of 13 follow-up respondents reported implementing at least one idea and while views of AI as beneficial were already positive and changed little, agreement that AI poses significant risks to academic integrity fell. These participant-reported, uncontrolled findings should be read as evidence of feasibility and perceived usefulness rather than causal impact.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in early-stage industrial design. It can quickly produce design concepts with strong visual expressiveness. However, these concepts often lack explicit dimensional parameters, material specifications, manufacturing routes, assembly definitions, and structural details. This creates considerable uncertainty for early manufacturability review. Some visual features in concept images may introduce manufacturing, assembly, or maintenance risks. At the same time, these features may also carry design intent related to appearance, functional recognition, interaction cues, or user experience. To address this issue, this study proposes Intent-Sensitive Manufacturability Review (ISMR). ISMR is a human-centered review framework that treats design intent as a soft constraint in early manufacturability review. It organizes visual cues, manufacturability risks, design-intent interpretation, potential intent loss, and required evidence for further verification in a structured manner. The proposed method is compared with an ordinary large language model (LLM)-based review and a traditional Design for Manufacturing (DFM) checklist-based review. The evaluation results show that ISMR performs more prominently in feature specificity and intent sensitivity. It can connect review issues more clearly with visible features in concept images. It also maintains attention to potential design intent when engineering risks are raised. Therefore, ISMR can serve as a useful complement to open-ended LLM review and checklist-based manufacturability review. It provides structured and intent-sensitive support for early design--engineering communication around AI-generated design concepts.

Digital communication has changed what counts as writing in higher education. Students compose across word processors, collaborative platforms, websites, presentations, infographics, video, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) environments, yet writing pedagogy often remains organized around monomodal print genres and sentence-level correctness. This conceptual article develops an integrated framework that connects Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL), the Genre-Based Approach (GBA), and digital multimodal composing (DMC). Using an integrative, theorybuilding design (Jabareen, 2009; Torraco, 2016) and a transparent literature procedure reported with reference to PRISMA 2020 principles (Page et al., 2021), the article synthesizes foundational works and 2021–2026 research in L2 writing, English for Academic Purposes, multimodality, and GenAI-mediated composition. Five research gaps are identified: limited integration of SFL genre pedagogy and DMC, weak alignment between multimodal tasks and assessment, an under-specified linguistic dimension of digital composing, limited transfer evidence, and misalignment between GenAI-supported composing and conventional assessment. In response, the article proposes an eight-phase SFLInformed Digital Genre Pedagogy framework and a six-dimension assessment architecture. Its novelty lies in aligning field–tenor–mode analysis, genre staging, and multimodal orchestration within one teaching–learning cycle; deriving assessment dimensions from the same phases; treating GenAI output as an object of functional-genre evaluation and verification; and adding a functional-sufficiency principle for metalanguage. Theoretical validity is argued through a traceability matrix and internal-consistency checks, and a staged protocol for empirical validation (expert review with content validity indices, rubric reliability, and argument-based validation) is specified. The framework is offered as a testable design architecture rather than an empirically validated model.

Given the importance of experiencing fulfilling and productive workdays, scholars have focused on ways to boost employees' daily engagement and performance, suggesting this may be accomplished by increasing meaningfulness of their work tasks. However, an alternative approach may be needed in multifaceted work contexts where employees need to complete sets of varied tasks each day, including tasks that lack meaningfulness. To address this issue, we integrate the workday design perspective with research on residual engagement to examine implications of strategically sequencing tasks in terms of their meaningfulness. We theorize that because of a process we refer to as engagement cascade, performing the day's most highly meaningful tasks earlier and in a concentrated manner will tend to produce higher levels of daily engagement relative to sequences in which the most highly meaningful tasks occur later or are disbursed. We use agent-based modeling to formalize the engagement cascade process and generate specific predictions regarding how daily engagement is impacted by different task meaningfulness sequences. Findings from an intensive longitudinal design study with National Aeronautics and Space Administration and Russian Space Agency crew members (Study 1), an experience sampling field experiment with full-time employees (Study 2), and two controlled laboratory experiments with undergraduates (Study 3 and Supplement to Study 3) provide support for our hypotheses. Specifically, the decreasing task meaningfulness sequence engendered higher levels of daily engagement and, in turn, daily performance, relative to the increasing, inverted U-shaped, and U-shaped sequences. Designing Learning That Adapts presents a practical framework for adaptive, scenario-based learning that can be applied across classrooms, e-learning platforms and AI-supported education. Drawing on established learning science, instructional design practice and the questions raised by more than a decade of e-learning product work, the paper sets out principles for shaping learning around the learner's goal, starting point, prior knowledge and preferred ways of learning, and for choosing the right mode (text, voice, video, interaction and dialogue) for each task. It frames adaptive and scenario-based approaches as design practices to be observed, tested and revised rather than as proven efficacy claims, and offers a structured way for educators, platform teams and workplace learning designers to apply these ideas in their own contexts. This is a practitioner framework and does not report an empirical efficacy study.

documents.abstract: This chapter explores the evolving, reciprocal relationship between leadership and augmented/artificial intelligence (AI) across individual, team, organizational, and societal levels. While we use the term AI throughout in recognition of its widespread usage, we acknowledge the growing preference for augmented intelligence – a framing advanced by leaders in human–machine teaming, such as Paul G. Kaminski (2020), which emphasizes cognitive extension and human–AI partnership. Just as leadership helped shape – and was reshaped by – the Agricultural, Industrial, and Information Ages, the emerging Age of AI demands a renewed focus on human values and moral courage. Far from a neutral tool, AI reflects the intentions of its designers and the integrity of its leaders, and in turn, transforms how we work, relate, and lead. Grounded in authentic and moral leadership theory, systems thinking, and sociotechnical design, we examine how leaders can engage AI in ways that safeguard human dignity, foster trust, and advance ethical innovation. Through a multilevel lens, we explore how AI influences self-awareness, interpersonal responsibility, team dynamics, and global leadership strategies. We extend prior work on efficacy-performance spirals to the AI context, showing how trust, learning, and adaptation can reinforce or erode across levels over time. Drawing on work published in Organizational Dynamics, this chapter also applies the TRUST, COACH, and CARES frameworks to AI leadership. As AI reshapes decision-making and connection, the defining force will not be technology itself, but the authenticity, trustworthiness, and moral imagination of those who lead it.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on proprietary system prompts to enforce task directives, safety policies, and access controls. These prompts are vulnerable to query-based leakage attacks, where black-box adversaries extract confidential instructions through adaptive, multi-turn interactions. Existing defenses often assess queries independently, missing malicious behavior that emerges across interactions. We present AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework for detecting and mitigating system prompt leakage. AdvGuard models cross-query relationships using a bounded semantic interaction graph, statistically filters candidate components, and converts them into line graphs for graph convolutional network (GCN) classification. This approach captures multi-hop patterns in query similarity that distinguish coordinated extraction from benign workflows. A lightweight prompt-level detector provides protection before sufficient interaction history accumulates, and the framework supports black-box LLM deployments. In mixed-query evaluations, AdvGuard improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline while maintaining a false positive rate of at most 3.4%. In multi-turn workloads, it achieves 97.23%-99.1% F1 with 100% recall. Leave-one-attack-family-out tests yield 99.98% mean recall and 99.99% mean F1, with no observed false positives. Integrated into the adaptive PLeak and LeakAgent attack loops, AdvGuard limits exact-match leakage to 0.00-0.01 and substring-match leakage to 0.01-0.09 across evaluated victim models. These results demonstrate robust detection of unseen attack families and substantially reduced prompt reconstruction.

documents.abstract: Relevance . Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) comprises a group of neurodevelopmental conditions requiring personalized approaches to developmental and educational support. Traditional approaches have limitations in terms of scalability and individualization. Objective . To analyze existing artificial intelligence (AI)-based solutions for supporting children with ASD and to describe the concept of a text-based intelligent system capable of dynamic learning and individualized adaptation. Methodology . Current AI-based solutions for supporting children with ASD were reviewed, including cognitive support platforms, conversational chatbots, robotic systems, and generative AI applications. An adaptive system architecture with a gamified interface was developed. Results . A concept for a text-based AI system was proposed that generates an individual child profile and adapts the difficulty, format, and content of tasks in real time. The system incorporates the principles of applied behavior analysis (ABA) and the Developmental, Individual-differences, Relationship-based (DIR)/Floortime approach at the level of its decision-making logic. Conclusion . The development of a text-based adaptive AI system represents a promising direction that combines advances in artificial intelligence with approaches to developmental and educational support.

documents.abstract: Continuous monitoring of aircraft flight data is vital for proactive aviation safety, air traffic management, and predictive maintenance. Traditional Flight Data Recorders (FDR) store parameters on-board, limiting data accessibility to post-flight or post-accident investigations. This paper presents the development of an interactive Ground Monitoring Console (GMC) and telemetry analytics framework tailored for general aviation flight operations. Utilizing the high-fidelity CAFUC2 multi-model aviation benchmark dataset collected from Cessna 172R aircraft sorties, we process and validate multi-parameter telemetry streams including altitude (Mean = 3,800.4 ft, Std = 1,312.6 ft), vertical speed climb/descent distributions (3,129 climb vs 3,418 descent samples), pitch/roll attitudes (Mean = 2.55° and 1.35°), engine speed (Mean = 1,930.2 RPM, Std = 223.4 RPM), fuel flow (Mean = 8.23 GPH), and 2D GPS spatial navigation trajectories. A multi-panel software console is designed to integrate live spectrum monitoring, Quadrature Phase Shift Keying (QPSK) constellation diagnostics (achieving 9.96% Error Vector Magnitude at 20 dB SNR), carrier signal quality indicators, and flight status displays. The framework provides ground controllers and flight safety officers with enhanced situational awareness and early warning capabilities without imposing heavy computational overhead. This foundational system establishes the baseline telemetry visualization architecture for future high-frequency RF front-ends.

This study investigates whether distinct “machine-translationese” and “LLM-translationese” exist in Chinese–English government translation by comparing DeepSeek V4Pro, Google neural machine translation, and pre-neural human translation. We built the corpus as 24 minimally overlapping 5,000-word windows per translation condition, yielding 72 matched observations. Using 21 normalized linguistic features selected exclusively within a group-aware training partition, five classifiers were trained and evaluated with a fully held-out, chunk-disjoint test set, and their stability was cross-checked with nested cross-validation and 50 repeated group-aware splits. Naive Bayes and Random Forest emerged as the most consistently above-chance classifiers, while the remaining classifiers were weaker or more sensitive to the specific partition. This indicates that the three translation agents are distinguishable from linguistic form alone. A five-factor multidimensional analysis identified discourse cohesion and causal-deictic linking as the strongest and most stable group contrast separating human translation from both machine systems, alongside four additional, comparatively weaker dimensions capturing nominal/lexical density, nominalization and wh-subordination, lexical diversity and dynamic aspect, and elaborative/predicative complexity. Corrected pairwise comparisons confirmed that human translation exceeds both machine systems on discourse cohesion, and that Google NMT and DeepSeek V4Pro are statistically indistinguishable from one another on most dimensions. A chunk-level bootstrap analysis confirmed that, in five-dimensional factor space, DeepSeek V4Pro and Google NMT sit reliably closer to each other than either does to human translation, supporting a shared machine-translationese distinct from institutional human translation. The study documents differences in stylistic profile and presents the proposed links to reader cognitive load and RLHF-driven hedging as hypotheses emerging from these structural findings. These results provide an empirically grounded, methodologically conservative basis for discussing LLM- and NMT-based translation in official contexts.

This research presents a literature review that investigates how digital competencies relate to student engagement, particularly in the integration of deep learning in primary education. Drawing on findings from a diverse range of peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2025, this review highlights that digital proficiency, including digital literacy, skills, and creativity, is closely associated with students’ cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement. The effective use of digital resources, such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and adaptive learning systems, promotes critical thinking and facilitates deep learning. The findings show that students with advanced digital capabilities demonstrate greater concentration and enthusiasm, whereas those with limited skills and autonomy are more likely to disengage and exhibit off-task behaviors online. Additional factors, such as personalized learning, social and emotional engagement, and teacher’s digital expertise also influence this relationship. Identified challenges include digital disparities, insufficient teacher preparation, and distractions from non-educational digital activities. To address these challenges, targeted digital literacy initiatives and improvements in curriculum design are recommended. In summary, this review highlights the complex relationship between digital competencies and student engagement, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive curriculum integration and teacher support to enhance learning outcomes through deep learning approaches in primary education.

As emerging adults (ages 18-30) figure out who they are and who they want to become, they often face the challenge of determining what career path to pursue. Many of them are also engaging with digital media, including conversational AI agents, while navigating these identity development processes. Although researchers recognize that identity develops in a digital context, little is known about how media can influence identity and its development. This study draws from past positive identity intervention research to better understand how digital media – and AI in particular — can be leveraged to support personal and vocational identity development. Here, we have developed and now aim to evaluate the efficacy of a digital intervention that consists of career-focused media prescriptions as treatments (i.e., AI reflection activities) that are designed to promote adaptive identity processes via reflection. We have recruited college students from the Bay Area into a randomized controlled trial to compare two active intervention conditions: (1) Self-Reflection (i.e., self-guided reflection activities) and (2) AI-mediated Reflection (i.e., AI chat reflection activities). The study design included between-person random assignment and within-person repeated measures collected before, during, and after the intervention. Our findings will show whether digital interventions incorporating reflection activities cause adaptive change in identity processes, while also demonstrating whether self-guided or AI-mediated reflection offers a promising approach for scaling developmental support for young people as they transition to adulthood.

Purpose This study aims to examine how women artisan entrepreneurs in northern Nigeria leverage digital technologies to pursue business opportunities and negotiate digital visibility within a conservative sociocultural context. This study also explores how digital entrepreneurship creates opportunities for market participation while remaining shaped by gendered social norms and constraints. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative case study approach based on semi-structured interviews with women artisan entrepreneurs operating in northern Nigeria. Findings The findings show how women artisans strategically use social media platforms, particularly Instagram and TikTok, to expand their market access, gain entrepreneurial knowledge, collaborate with peers and balance business with family responsibilities. However, they negotiate these opportunities within a conservative sociocultural environment that shapes their mobility, digital visibility and customer interactions, while also exposing them to online harassment and other gendered digital risks. Practical implications The study suggests that entrepreneurship support initiatives should move beyond improving digital access to strengthening women’s digital capabilities through training in social media marketing, customer relationship management, artificial intelligence and digital safety. Policies should also address gender-specific online risks through accessible reporting mechanisms and stronger platform-level trust and verification systems. Originality/value To the best of the author’s knowledge, this study provides one of the first in-depth qualitative analyses of women artisan entrepreneurs’ use of digital technologies in northern Nigeria. It advances artisan entrepreneurship and cyberfeminism scholarship by showing how women strategically navigate digital opportunities and sociocultural constraints, offering a contextually grounded understanding of digital entrepreneurship.

The digital era has reached a new inflection point, accelerated by artificial intelligence (AI) and organizations’ need to adapt to dynamic, technology-driven conditions. This chapter examines the legacy of Digital Transformation 1.0—highlighting failures and their causes—and defines the imperatives of AI-infused Digital Transformation 2.0. Drawing from relevant case studies, research, and executive interviews, it emphasizes the critical shift from episodic digitization to sustained AI-embedded digitalization. Leaders must enable systems-level transformation across people, process, and technology while aligning cultural, ethical, and operational domains. Digital Transformation 2.0 demands coordinated iterative design over monolithic strategy, requiring organizations to reimagine work as a fluid mix of tasks rather than fixed roles. Human–AI collaboration is a new reality that depends on psychological safety, AI literacy, and digital dexterity across the blended human-AI workforce. Successful transformation hinges on new leadership behaviors that elevate trust, agency, and adaptability while modeling and encouraging the use of new tools. The piece explores decentralized workforce models, the urgency of building AI-ready cultures, and a new social contract. It examines how agile frameworks, value mapping, and upskilling efforts create coherence amid complexity, making change tangible and participatory. The Future of Work is framed not as a fixed destination, but as a dynamic system requiring deliberate, ongoing leadership to combine machine capabilities with uniquely human capabilities. Ultimately, this work calls for defining or reframing organizational purpose and progress: AI can multiply what we value, but it is up to us to define what we value—and how we lead with it.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: A digital twin is a virtual replica of a physical entity that is continuously updated with real-world data and can be used to analyse, predict and test outcomes without risk to the original. Originally developed for aerospace and manufacturing, the concept is now being adapted to healthcare, where the twin may represent a single organ, an entire patient or a hospital. Conventional care relies on population averages, periodic check-ups and trial-and-error treatment, which leaves gaps in personalisation, early detection and safety. This paper reviews the concept of the healthcare digital twin, its enabling technologies (wearable sensors, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, medical imaging and health records, and 5G networks), a generic working architecture, and major application areas including personalised medicine, surgical planning, chronic disease management, drug development and hospital operations. It further discusses live patient monitoring, benefits, data privacy and regulatory considerations (HIPAA, GDPR and India’s DPDP Act 2023), and open challenges of cost, interoperability, workforce readiness and biological complexity. The review concludes that digital twins can make healthcare more predictive, personalised and safer, provided that privacy, standardisation and affordability are addressed.

documents.abstract: This article examines how generative artificial intelligence (AI) assistants can strengthen Lean Six Sigma (LSS) execution across every phase of the Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control (DMAIC) methodology. The objective is to give LSS practitioners field-tested patterns, quantified cycle-time data, and a governance framework for integrating AI assistants into quality-improvement projects without compromising methodological rigor. The investigation draws on recent industry deployments using Anthropic’s Claude assistant and a construct called skills: versioned playbooks that bundle written instructions, scripts, reference data, and validation rules into reusable artifacts. Methods include direct measurement of cycle-time deltas across Define, Measure, and Control tasks; four worked Analyze-phase examples spanning hypothesis testing, Measurement System Analysis, Statistical Process Control, and regression interpretation; and analysis of a multi-skill portfolio deployed at a small aviation services client. Results demonstrate substantial efficiency gains: project-charter drafting time fell from 90 to 120 minutes to roughly 6 minutes; monthly payroll consolidation fell from 90 minutes to under 30 seconds (a 99.4 percent reduction) with the first-pass error rate dropping to zero; cross-system benefits reconciliation fell from 4 hours to under 60 seconds, with monthly completion improving from 5 of 12 cycles to 12 of 12. The aggregate skills portfolio at one client achieved approximately 84 hours of administrative cycle-time savings per year. The article identifies six required governance controls (human review, version control, controlled prompts, sensitive-data boundaries, hallucination mitigation, and auditability) and aligns them with ISO 9001: 2015 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The conclusion is that generative AI does not alter DMAIC methodology; it lowers the cost of executing each phase well, expanding the share of LSS that is practiced in fact rather than only in theory. The findings support Master Black Belts and quality champions in deliberately piloting AI-enabled tooling, prioritizing Control-phase tasks first, and treating skill development as a formal deliverable with version control, ownership, and quality gates.

documents.abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.

documents.abstract: Generative AI tools are now routinely used by Chinese Language and Literature majors for tasks once considered the province of individual literary craft: drafting verse, shaping narrative prose, revising fiction. Two competing accounts describe what this means for students’ confidence in their own creative writing. A cognitive-offloading account holds that repeated reliance on AI displaces the mastery experiences through which writing self-efficacy is built, so reliance erodes confidence over time. A compensatory-use account holds the reverse: students whose confidence is already low turn to AI to avoid the discomfort of unassisted composition, so low confidence drives reliance. Cross-sectional and standard cross-lagged designs cannot separate these accounts because they confound stable between-person differences with genuine within-person change. We addressed this using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) across four waves spanning one academic year among Chinese Language and Literature undergraduates ( N = 390 recruited; N = 387 analyzed under full-information maximum likelihood, of whom 298 supplied complete four-wave data). Generative AI writing reliance (GAWR) and literary creative writing self-efficacy (LCWSE) were assessed at each wave. The trait-level association between the two constructs was negative and could not be distinguished from zero ( r = −.342, Δχ²(1) = 2.26, p = .133). At the within-person level, declines in self-efficacy predicted subsequent increases in reliance (β = −.276, p < .001). The reverse path, from reliance to subsequent self-efficacy, was smaller and fell short of the conventional threshold (β = −.085, p = .072). We state explicitly that this second result is not interpretable as evidence against erosion: a Monte Carlo power analysis put this design's power to detect an effect of that magnitude at 53.2%, close to a coin flip, so the erosion pathway is undetermined in these data and this null supplies no basis for concluding that erosion does not operate. A direct comparison of the two cross-lagged paths favored compensation (Δχ²(1) = 8.83, p = .003; bootstrap 95% CI for the difference [.020, .218] across 5,000 resamples), with the qualification that this comparison sets an adequately powered estimate against an underpowered one and therefore describes what this design was able to detect. Compensation is the pathway this study establishes; whether reliance also erodes confidence over a longer horizon is an open question. We discuss implications for writing pedagogy in Chinese Language and Literature programs and for how underpowered null results should be interpreted in AI-in-education panel research.

Generative bundle construction completes a partially observed bundle by generating its missing items from a large product catalog. Compared to autoregressive LLMs, diffusion LLM emerges as a natural fit for this unordered generation task. Their bidirectional attention provides an inductive bias better aligned with unordered bundle construction. Iterative denoising can reveal multiple tokens per step, potentially reducing inference latency. However, directly applying DLMs to this task presents two key challenges: 1 Despite its flexible reveal order, confidence-guided decoding tends to postpone semantic-fork decisions until refinement tokens constrain their choices, reducing bundle diversity. 2 Revealing more tokens per step can compromise recommendation quality, stifling the potential for faster inference. We introduce DPE-Rec, a diffusion framework for diversity preservation and efficient recommendation. DPE-Rec preserves diversity by introducing semantic-fork-aware GRPO, which prioritizes semantic-fork decisions via autoregressive rollouts. It improves efficiency through pseudo-trajectory distillation, which concentrates learning from the vast random corruption space onto the compact trajectory-induced subspace visited by high-quality decoding, unlocking reliable multi-token decoding. Together, these components enable diverse and accurate bundle construction with substantially fewer denoise steps. Experiments on multiple bundle construction benchmarks show that DPE-Rec improves recommendation performance by 63% on average, and its fast variant achieves 25.6$times$ faster inference on average than existing generative recommendation arts, with minimal loss in recommendation quality.

World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.

Battery management systems (BMSs) increasingly require low-latency, reliable, and intelligent processing capabilities to support the rapid expansion of electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. Conventional centralized and cloud-dependent BMS architectures can provide advanced analytics but may face limitations associated with communication latency, network dependence, data transmission overhead, and privacy. Edge artificial intelligence (Edge AI) provides an alternative approach by performing data processing and intelligent inference close to the battery system. This review examines major technology trends in real-time BMSs and proposes a reference design framework for Edge AI-based battery management. Recent developments in battery sensing, artificial intelligence-based state estimation, decentralized computing, lightweight machine learning, digital twins, communication, and cybersecurity are reviewed. Based on these trends, a layered framework is proposed in which battery sensors and embedded controllers acquire operating data, edge processors perform preprocessing and intelligent analysis, and cloud platforms provide long-term data management, model updating, and fleet-level analytics. The framework emphasizes local state estimation, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, secure edge-cloud communication, and optional digital-twin integration. The review indicates that Edge AI can reduce dependence on continuous cloud connectivity and enable faster decision-making, although practical deployment remains constrained by limited embedded resources, model complexity, cybersecurity risks, heterogeneous battery platforms, and interoperability issues. Future BMS development is expected to combine lightweight AI, adaptive edge-cloud collaboration, explainable decision support, digital twins, and security-by-design principles.

Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui efektivitas penggunaan media counting box terhadap keterlibatan siswa dan hasil belajar matematika siswa kelas I SD. Pendekatan kuantitatif digunakan dengan desain pre-eksperimental one group pretest-posttest design, melibatkan 25 siswa kelas I SD. Uji normalitas Kolmogorov-Smirnov menghasilkan nilai signifikansi 0,210 (p > 0,05). Rata-rata nilai pretest adalah 58,4 dan posttest 88,2. Analisis N-Gain menghasilkan nilai rata-rata 0,72 berkategori Tinggi. Keterlibatan siswa mencapai rata-rata 88,6% (Sangat Tinggi) yang mencakup dimensi perilaku (92%), emosional (86%), dan kognitif (88%). Media counting box efektif mengubah konsep abstrak berhitung menjadi pengalaman manipulatif konkret yang sesuai tahap perkembangan kognitif operasional konkret siswa kelas I SD. abstract This study aims to examine the effectiveness of counting box media on student engagement and mathematics learning outcomes in Grade I elementary school. A quantitative approach was employed using a pre-experimental one group pretest-posttest design with 25 Grade I students as research subjects. Data were collected through pretest and posttest instruments, student engagement observation sheets, and questionnaires. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test yielded a significance value of 0.210 (p > 0.05), confirming normally distributed data. The mean pretest score was 58.4, which increased to 88.2 on the posttest. N-Gain analysis produced a mean score of 0.72, classified as High, indicating significant improvement in learning outcomes. Student engagement reached an average of 88.6% (Very High), comprising behavioral engagement (92%), emotional engagement (86%), and cognitive engagement (88%). These findings demonstrate that counting box media is effective in transforming abstract arithmetic concepts into concrete manipulative experiences aligned with the operational concrete cognitive development stage of Grade I students.
topics: Cognitive and developmental aspects of mathematical skills

documents.abstract: Clinical decision-making in patients receiving antiresorptive medications requires balancing tooth preservation against the risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ). This study compared the performance of ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek in MRONJ-related endodontic scenarios and evaluated the effect of guideline-assisted prompting using the 2022 American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons Position Paper. Eighteen fictional and standardized MRONJ-related endodontic clinical scenarios were developed based on the 2022 AAOMS Position Paper and current scientific evidence. Three contemporary LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek) were evaluated using a two-phase study design consisting of baseline and guideline-assisted assessments. In the second phase, the complete AAOMS Position Paper was provided before evaluation of the same scenarios. Two endodontic specialists independently scored the anonymized responses across five clinical decision-making domains using a six-point ordinal scale (0–5). The primary outcome was the mean of the five domain scores, yielding an overall clinical decision-making score ranging from 0 to 5. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using the initial ratings, and disagreements were resolved through consensus before analysis. Linear mixed models (LMMs) were used for the primary analyses, with cumulative link mixed models (CLMMs) performed as sensitivity analyses for the ordinal domain scores. Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons were performed where appropriate. At baseline, ChatGPT achieved a significantly higher mean overall score than Claude (4.68 ± 0.14 vs. 4.29 ± 0.38). Following guideline-assisted prompting, Claude’s mean score increased to 4.68 ± 0.28 (+ 0.39 points on the 0–5 scale), and the statistically significant difference between ChatGPT and Claude was no longer observed. DeepSeek consistently received lower overall scores than both models. A significant overall phase effect ( p < 0.001) and model-by-phase interaction ( p = 0.004) were identified. Domain-level CLMM sensitivity analyses generally supported the LMM findings, although the phase effect for consultation and medication management was not confirmed by the CLMM. The most pronounced model-specific increase in guideline-concordant scores was observed for follow-up recommendations, particularly for Claude. Guideline-assisted prompting was associated with higher concordance with the predefined reference standard, particularly for Claude, which showed the largest improvement in overall scores and follow-up recommendations. Although ChatGPT scored significantly higher than Claude at baseline, this difference was no longer statistically significant following guideline-assisted prompting. Because the clinical scenarios, reference standard, and guideline-assisted intervention were aligned with the same AAOMS guideline, these findings should not be interpreted as independent validation of clinical accuracy. Further studies using externally developed scenarios and real-world clinical cases are required before considering these models for clinician-supervised decision support.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Skin cancer ranks among mostly prevalent cancer types across the globe, and its treatment outcomes and survival rates show improvement through early detection methods which achieve precise results. The traditional methods of diagnosis depend on visual assessment and clinical expertise, which creates a risk of delayed detection and erroneous diagnosis. Using a specially selected dataset, this study suggests an effective deep learning-based method with data augmentation for the separation of skin cancer disorders in order to overcome these difficulties. Regarding the categorization of skin lesions into different groups, we have used CNN in conjunction with transfer learning models like VGG16 and VGG19. A balanced, specially created dataset of annotated skin lesion photos was used to train and evaluate the models. To increase generalization and model resilience, preprocessing methods and data augmentation were used. With a classification accuracy of up to 97% suggested system shows promising outcomes for high-precision faster medical diagnosis. Additionally, a comparative analysis of various models was carried out, emphasizing of trade-offs among training complexity, accuracy, computational efficiency. The potential of deep learning to provide dermatologists and other medical practitioners with automated, dependable, and scalable skin cancer detection systems is demonstrated through this study. Also Multimodal LLM Based Model is used for classification of diseases more accurately.

An der BiblioCon 2026 in Berlin stellten wir unsere ganzsemestrige Lehrveranstaltung „Scientific Information Literacy“ vor, die von der Universitätsbibliothek Zürich für Studierende der Biowissenschaften angeboten wird. Dieser jährlich wiederkehrende Kurs vermittelt zentrale Kompetenzen der wissenschaftlichen Informationskompetenz, greift aktuelle Entwicklungen wie generative KI auf und kombiniert unterschiedliche Lehr- und Prüfungsformate. Am Beispiel des Kurses wird gezeigt, wie Liaison Librarianship dazu beitragen kann, bibliothekarische Lehrangebote gemeinsam mit den Fakultäten weiterzuentwickeln und langfristig in Studienprogramme einzubetten.At the BiblioCon 2026 in Berlin, we presented “Scientific Information Literacy”, a semester-long course offered by the University Library Zurich for students in the life sciences. This annual course teaches key concepts of scientific information literacy, addresses current developments such as generative artificial intelligence, and combines a variety of teaching and assessment formats. Using this course as an example, we suggest that liaison librarianship can contribute to the development of library-led educational offerings in close collaboration with the faculties of the university and support their long-term integration into curricula.

Health education has emerged as an essential component in the management of cardiovascular disease (CVD), especially in contexts where physical access to medical care may be limited. This study, conducted in Ibagué, Colombia, evaluated the role of emerging technologies in improving education for both patients and health professionals. Through expert interviews, technology watch, and the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), five technologies were prioritized for institutional implementation in cardiovascular care; their educational potential for patients and healthcare professionals was then analyzed as a complementary dimension. The results highlighted the educational impact of 3D model-ling, telemedicine, and artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical triage and in teaching complex cardiac conditions. The findings suggest that 3D modelling and printing, telemedicine, remote monitoring, and AI-supported tools have relevant educational potential in cardiovascular care. In particular, 3D-printed cardiac models may help improve patient understanding of complex conditions and may contribute to reducing uncertainty and supporting treatment adherence. Telemedicine and remote monitoring may facilitate autonomous learning, self-care, and patient empowerment, while AI applied to electrocardiogram analysis may support professional training through automated feedback and decision-support processes. In conclusion, the strategic integration of emerging technologies could strengthen cardiovascular education, support clinical communication, and contribute to better-informed care processes, provided that these tools are implemented with adequate infrastructure, professional training, and patient-centred educational strategies.

documents.abstract: Global banking and investment operations are changing as financial institutions adopt new technologies, expand into international markets, and strengthen risk management. Banks and investment firms must process transactions accurately, protect financial data, meet regulatory requirements, and deliver reliable services to clients across different regions. These changes are creating new expectations for banking operations professionals. In addition to financial knowledge, employers increasingly need people who understand data analysis, digital tools, compliance procedures, and process improvement. Automation is also changing routine tasks, which increases the value of skills in exception handling, analytical thinking, and operational control. India has become an important centre for global financial services and technology-enabled business operations. Hyderabad and Bengaluru are key locations in this ecosystem, with companies supporting financial processes, technology development, risk management, and business services. The changing landscape of global banking operations Global banking operations include the processes that support financial transactions across markets. These processes help financial institutions record trades, transfer funds and securities, maintain accurate data, and meet regulatory obligations. Operations teams work with front-office, middle-office, compliance, finance, and technology departments. Their responsibilities may include trade confirmation, settlement support, reconciliation, corporate actions, transaction monitoring, and financial reporting. Several forces are changing this work: The growth of cross-border transactions and international financial services. Greater use of automation and artificial intelligence. Increased focus on data quality and operational efficiency. Stronger requirements for risk management and regulatory compliance. Expansion of Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India. Rising demand for digital and analytical skills. These developments mean that banking operations are no longer limited to routine transaction processing. Many teams now support analysis, control monitoring, technology adoption, and process improvement. Artificial intelligence and intelligent automation Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the main forces changing financial operations. Banks can use AI-based tools to review documents, classify information, detect unusual transaction patterns, and support customer service. Robotic process automation can also handle repetitive, rule-based tasks. The shift is moving from small pilot projects towards wider use across business functions. An EY India GCC Pulse Survey published in November 2025 reported that 58% of surveyed Indian GCCs were investing in agentic AI, while 83% were investing in generative AI. The survey also found that 81% were upskilling internal teams in generative AI. These findings indicate growing interest in both technology adoption and workforce development. For banking operations, automation can reduce manual data entry and support faster processing. However, automated systems still require oversight. Professionals must review exceptions, check outputs, identify errors, and follow approved controls. This creates a need for skills in process analysis, data validation, workflow monitoring, and risk awareness. Learners considering Certification In Global & Investment Banking Operations (CGIBO) in Hyderabad should look for opportunities to understand how modern banking processes use technology while maintaining accuracy and control. Data analytics and real-time financial reporting Financial institutions generate large amounts of data through payments, securities transactions, customer activity, and regulatory reporting. Data analytics helps operations teams turn this information into useful insights. Instead of relying only on manual checks, teams can use dashboards and analytical tools to monitor transaction volumes, identify processing delays, and detect recurring errors. This can help managers improve workflows and allocate resources more effectively. Important developments in this area include: Real-time monitoring: Tracking transactions and operational performance as events occur. Predictive analytics: Using historical data to identify possible risks and processing problems. Automated reporting: Reducing repetitive work and improving consistency. Data quality management: Checking records for missing, incorrect, or inconsistent information. Business intelligence: Presenting operational results through reports and dashboards. These capabilities are useful across trade support, reconciliation, risk operations, and financial reporting. Professionals who understand financial processes and can interpret data may be better prepared for roles that require both operational knowledge and analytical thinking. Learners researching Certification In Global & Investment Banking Operations (CGIBO) in Bangalore can review the programme curriculum to determine whether it covers relevant financial concepts, reporting processes, and practical applications. Stronger compliance and financial crime prevention Regulatory compliance remains a major priority for banks and investment firms. Financial institutions must follow applicable laws, protect customer information, maintain accurate records, and monitor transactions for suspicious activity. Know Your Customer (KYC), Anti-Money Laundering (AML), customer due diligence, sanctions screening, and fraud prevention are important parts of this work. A report published by the India Brand Equity Foundation in July 2025, citing Careernet research, stated that India's financial crime talent pool had grown to more than 25,500 professionals. The report identified Bengaluru as the largest centre in this talent pool, accounting for 32%, while Hyderabad accounted for 17%. It also highlighted demand across customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, fraud control, and regulatory compliance. These figures reflect the importance of specialised compliance skills in India's financial services ecosystem. They do not guarantee that vacancies will be available to every candidate, but they indicate areas worth monitoring when planning a career. Technology is also changing compliance work. Automated screening tools can help identify unusual activity, while data analytics can support investigations. Human review remains important because alerts need context, documentation, and appropriate escalation. Professionals who combine knowledge of financial transactions with compliance awareness can explore opportunities in KYC operations, AML support, transaction monitoring, and financial crime prevention. Expansion of Global Capability Centres in India Global Capability Centres have become an important part of the international financial services industry. These centres support multinational companies through functions such as transaction processing, finance, analytics, risk management, technology development, and compliance. Their responsibilities are also changing. Many organisations are moving beyond routine support work towards specialised activities that contribute to global business decisions and innovation. A 2026 report by The Economic Times described how Indian GCCs were expanding their use of AI and creating demand for specialised skills that combine technology, business knowledge, and strategy. This development matters for people entering banking operations. Employers may need professionals who can understand financial processes, work with digital systems, interpret data, and identify opportunities to improve workflows. India's GCC ecosystem also creates opportunities for continuous professional development. Employees may gain experience in international processes, cross-functional teamwork, and global operating standards. Hyderabad and Bengaluru are relevant locations for learners exploring these career paths. However, specific opportunities depend on employer requirements, qualifications, work experience, and the skills expected for each position. Multinational companies use the city to support activities across financial services, analytics, technology, and business operations. This environment is relevant to professionals interested in trade processing, financial reporting, compliance, risk operations, and technology-enabled services. Some roles focus on daily transaction workflows, while others involve reporting, data quality, or process improvement.
