Low-precision arithmetic can make reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models cheaper, but RL requires the sampler and the learner to agree. Several frameworks now run FP8 on both sides. We implement end-to-end MXFP8 RL in verl (Megatron/Transformer Engine training; vLLM and SGLang rollout; dense and MoE models) and measure on B200 GPUs, with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, what this design buys, when it is faster, and how it fails. (1) Matching. For an MXFP8 learner, a sampler on the learner's grid is more consistent than a higher-precision BF16 sampler: in one engine at fixed weights, train-rollout KL is 11% lower with half of the sampler's linear layers on the grid and 16% lower with all of them, and the synchronized weights we checked equal the learner's FP8 forward weights byte for byte. On the MoE model, an FP8 pipeline whose sampler uses another grid has twice the shared-grid pipeline's KL from the first step. Without a quantized KV cache, BF16 end to end remains 2.5-10x more consistent. (2) Speed. MXFP8 training adds a fixed cost per micro-batch and saves a per-token cost, so in our dense setting it pays off only above about 4.5k tokens per micro-batch; a micro-batch sweep on identical data confirms the per-micro-batch cost, and a trace shows the GPU waiting for the host for most of the added time. End to end, MXFP8 cuts MoE step time by 10.7% and generation time by 24%, and slows a short-sequence dense workload by 5%. (3) Correctness. We state seven conditions every weight synchronization must preserve and checks that test them against the live engine. Each of the seven failures we met on hardware broke one condition, five silently; the checks caught two at their first opportunity, each missed by the other checks, and CPU fault-injection tests reproduce five. All runs are single-seed and at most 60 steps long; we make no claim about final model quality.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence is a key driver of economic growth and sustainable development for modern economies. Its development relies heavily on enabling conditions such as access to electricity, globalization, openness, effective regulatory quality, and skilled human capital. This study examined the dynamic relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) and energy access, as well as the impact of globalization, human development, regulatory quality, and globalization policy on AI development in Africa. It covered 2015 to 2023 and used the System Generalized Method of Moments. Employing panel data, it adopted a reverse approach to existing studies to examine the impact of energy poverty on AI and determined the moderating effect of regulatory quality, globalization policy, and energy poverty on AI adoption. Its main objective is to examine the dynamic influence of energy poverty on Artificial Intelligence in Africa and contribute evidence relevant to the UN Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 9. Findings show that energy access significantly undermines Artificial Intelligence development. It further revealed that globalization and human development are negative and insignificant determinants of AI development, while regulatory quality exhibits a marginally significant ( p -value = 0.057) support for AI development. Further findings reveal that the synergistic interaction between energy access and globalization policy significantly reduced the impact of energy access on AI development. Meanwhile, the marginal negative effect of the interaction between energy access and regulatory quality on AI development is insignificant. The study recommends the prioritization of affordable and reliable energy, a shift from general to strategic globalization, AI skill-related development programs, quality institutions, effective integration policies , and enabling conditions to improve AI in Africa.

Motivating students has long been a challenge for physical educators, a problem exacerbated by declining physical activity rates among school-age youth. As physical education is often a child’s first structured exposure to physical activity, effective instruction that intrinsically motivates youth is crucial for cultivating healthy and active lifestyles. Student motivation in physical education can be understood as the direction and intensity of participation, influenced by intrinsic and extrinsic factors frequently determined by teacher actions. Extrinsic motivators often fall short of building long-term commitment from students, while lasting engagement in physical activity, both inside and outside of the gymnasium, stems from students’ intrinsic motivation to participate. Effective physical education teachers must be intentional in selecting and utilizing pedagogical strategies that not only motivate students to learn but also encourage them to develop their own intrinsic motivation for lifelong physical activity. This article discusses motivational theories and their role in creating an environment that inspires students to perform, persist, and grow. It presents popular theories of motivation relevant to physical education, along with applied pedagogical strategies aligned with each theory to support the development of intrinsically motivated students.
topics: Physical education and sports games research

documents.abstract: Sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks target ultra-high data rates, sub-millisecond latencies, and centimeterto-millimeter-level positioning accuracy. This unprecedented localization precision is essential for missioncritical applications such as autonomous transportation, smart grids, extended reality (XR), and industrial automation. However, operating at high frequencies (millimeter-wave and Terahertz bands) exposes 6G signals to severities including rapid path loss, signal blockages, and complex multipath interference. Traditional geometric and range-based methods face fundamental performance ceilings under these non-line-of-sight (NLoS) and dynamic channel conditions. This paper proposes a hybrid, artificial intelligence-assisted localization framework to solve these challenges. We design a multi-layer feedforward backpropagation Artificial Neural Network (ANN) trained on multi-path Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) profiles. To tackle high-velocity user equipment (UE) tracking in dense urban centers, we deploy a self-tuning Kalman Filter (KF) configured directly over the raw neural network predictions. We evaluate our design in a simulated100m equilateral 6G base station grid. Under dynamic shadowing conditions (1.5 dB) and high velocity (35 m/s or 126 km/h), the proposed hybrid model successfully reduces the mean physical positioning error from 7.970 meters (baseline static ANN) to 4.380 meters—achieving a substantial 45.04% improvement in tracking accuracy and a 41.83% improvement in the 90th percentile bounds (down to 7.793 meters). These empirical results validate the robustness of blending low-overhead AI models with temporal kinetic filters, supporting high-fidelity location services in next-generation networks.

This study aimed to examine the effect of Small Group Discussion supported by ChatGPT Voice on student’s speaking skills at SMPN 4 Koto Baru. A quantitative approach with a pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design was employed. The participants considered of 27 seventh-grade A student’s selected through total sampling. Data were collected using speaking tests assessing pronunciation, fluency, vocabulary, and grammar. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, and Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test. The results showed that the students mean score increased from 34.81 in the pre-test and 44.44 in the post-test. The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test yielded a significance value of 0.000 (p < 0.05). Therefore, the null hypothesis (H0) was rejected, and the alternative hypothesis (Ha) was accepted. Indicating that Small Group Discussion supported by ChatGPT Voice has a significant positive effect on students speaking skills. These findings suggest that integrating collaborative learning with AI-assisted speaking practice can serve as an effective strategy for improving students speaking skills.

Abstract The Transport Research and Innovation Monitoring and Information System (TRIMIS) tracks EU-funded transport research and innovation projects to identify trends and inform policymaking. A key function of TRIMIS is maintaining a comprehensive and accurate database of transport projects. Selecting and categorising relevant projects is a manual and time-consuming process. This study explores the use of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically large language models (LLMs), to support and accelerate this task. A workflow was developed using an LLM platform (GENESIS, the JRC internal, secure, general-purpose LLM platform), iteratively refining prompts to match expert human judgment in identifying relevant projects from CORDIS. Comparing LLM-generated outputs to the existing TRIMIS database, projects were assessed for inclusion/exclusion and classified by transport mode and sector, and technology thematic area. The classifications allow for filtering and consequent analysis and visualisation by these categories. A further application investigated was the assessment of projects for their contribution to the competitiveness of the EU Automotive Industry. Prompt engineering iterations and structured output analysis improved accuracy and consistency and reduced the risk of unsupported or fabricated classifications by requiring every positive decision to be grounded in a verbatim quotation from the project text. Using the ensemble configuration, we analysed 52,923 Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe projects (2014–2026), identifying 6,986 relevant for inclusion in the TRIMIS database, with reporting in this paper focused on the most recent 19,025 Horizon Europe projects, of which 2,184 (11.5%) were assessed as relevant. The analysis of the full corpus required about two days of serial model time for the two deployed configurations (Annex 5), reducing manual work and identifying matches in previously overlooked funding sources. Outcomes also helped to re-evaluate existing taxonomies. The results demonstrate the potential of AI-assisted workflows to reduce manual workload, improve accuracy, and scale project curation for the TRIMIS database, with broader implications for using AI-assisted methods in public-sector knowledge management. Future work will explore hybrid human-AI review pipelines and domain-specific fine-tuning.

EPT E INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFIOS E POSSIBILIDADES PARA A FORMAÇÃO DE PROFISSIONAIS NA ERA DIGITAL. VOCATIONAL AND TECHNOLOGICAL EDUCATION AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: CHALLENGES AND POSSIBILITIES FOR PROFESSIONAL TRAINING IN THE DIGITAL AGE. EDUCACIÓN PROFESIONAL Y TECNOLÓGICA E INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL: DESAFÍOS Y POSIBILIDADES PARA LA FORMACIÓN DE PROFESIONALES EN LA ERA DIGITAL. Gabriel Nascimento de Carvalho Simone Helen Drumond Ischkanian Gladys Nogueira Cabral Celine Maria de Sousa Azevedo Silvana Nascimento de Carvalho Sygride Nascimento de Carvalho Sandro Garabed Ischkanian RESUMO A Educação Profissional e Tecnológica (EPT) enfrenta desafios relacionados à incorporação da inteligência artificial nos processos de ensino e aprendizagem, na organização curricular e no desenvolvimento de competências necessárias ao mundo do trabalho. A expansão das tecnologias digitais demanda reflexões sobre as possibilidades de inovação pedagógica, a preparação dos docentes, a formação crítica dos estudantes e as implicações éticas do uso de sistemas inteligentes. Diante desse cenário, estabelece-se como problema de pesquisa: de que maneira a inteligência artificial pode contribuir para a formação de profissionais na EPT, considerando as exigências da transformação digital e os desafios de sua implementação educacional? O objetivo geral consiste em analisar os desafios e as possibilidades da integração da inteligência artificial à formação profissional, com atenção às competências técnicas, digitais, críticas e éticas requeridas na contemporaneidade. Metodologicamente, propõe-se uma pesquisa qualitativa, de caráter exploratório e descritivo, desenvolvida por meio de revisão bibliográfica e análise documental de publicações científicas e documentos institucionais pertinentes à temática. A análise permite discutir possibilidades de personalização da aprendizagem, apoio às atividades pedagógicas, simulação de situações profissionais e aproximação entre educação e transformações tecnológicas. Também evidencia desafios relativos à infraestrutura, à formação docente, à proteção de dados, aos vieses algorítmicos e às desigualdades de acesso. Conclui-se que a integração da inteligência artificial à EPT requer planejamento pedagógico, formação continuada e princípios éticos, de modo a articular inovação tecnológica, inclusão educacional e desenvolvimento humano na preparação dos profissionais para a era digital. Palavras-chave: Educação profissional e tecnológica; inteligência artificial; formação profissional; competências digitais. ABSTRACT Professional and Technological Education (PTE) faces challenges related to the incorporation of artificial intelligence into teaching and learning processes, curriculum organization, and the development of skills required in the world of work. The expansion of digital technologies calls for reflection on the possibilities of pedagogical innovation, teacher preparation, students’ critical development, and the ethical implications of using intelligent systems. Against this background, the research problem is formulated as follows: how can artificial intelligence contribute to professional training in PTE, considering the demands of digital transformation and the challenges of its educational implementation? The general objective is to analyze the challenges and possibilities of integrating artificial intelligence into professional education, focusing on the technical, digital, critical, and ethical competencies required in contemporary society. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive approach, based on a literature review and documentary analysis of scientific publications and institutional documents relevant to the topic. The analysis discusses opportunities for personalized learning, support for pedagogical activities, simulation of professional situations, and closer alignment between education and technological change. It also identifies challenges involving infrastructure, teacher training, data protection, algorithmic bias, and unequal access. The study concludes that integrating artificial intelligence into PTE requires pedagogical planning, continuing professional development, and ethical principles to connect technological innovation, educational inclusion, and human development in preparing professionals for the digital age. Keywords: Professional and technological education; artificial intelligence; professional training; digital competencies. Background: Juvenile (adolescent) girls from socio-economically disadvantaged households continue to perform heavy manual material-handling (MMH) tasks in India’s unorganized brick-manufacturing sector, despite legal protections against child labour. Evidence on their ergonomic exposures, physiological strain, and musculoskeletal health remains scarce. Objective: To evaluate the physical workload, postural stress, thermal exposure, musculoskeletal symptom prevalence, and acute physiological responses of juvenile girls employed in manual brick manufacturing units in West Bengal, India. Methods: A cross-sectional study design was adopted involving 100 young females within the age group of 13 to 18 years who worked at brick manufacturing plants in Nadia and Howrah districts of West Bengal. Data collection included interviews using modified Nordic questionnaires, anthropometry, activity observations both direct and video recorded, postural analysis through the Ovako Working Posture Analysis System (OWAS), thermal environment assessment, and physiological parameters both pre and post tasks of brick carrying. A paired t-test was performed to assess the physiological parameters before and after brick carrying, while the chi-square test was used to determine any relationship between musculoskeletal symptoms and BMI or the number of bricks handled per day. Results: The mean age was 15.5±2.33 years, BMI was 18.90±1.52 kg/m² and the occupational experience was 1.3±0.6 years. In general, 91% of participants complained of job-related pain, including the head (72%), neck (72%), and leg (78%). Neck pain was statistically correlated with chronic energy deficiencies (BMI < 18.5 kg/m², χ² = 9.675, p = 0.0019). Lifting more than 2,000 bricks per day was statistically correlated with head pain (χ² = 6.722, p = 0.0095), neck pain (χ² = 4.228, p = 0.0397), shoulder pain (χ² = 4.396, p = 0.0360), and back pain (χ² = 10.306, p = 0.0013). Bricks lifting led to a significant increase in heart rate (from 80.33±3.67 to 112.45±2.13 beats/min, p < 0.05), systolic blood pressure (from 119.7±3.5 to 134.9±5.15 mmHg, p < 0.05), and perceived exertion level (from 13.2±1.5 to 18.6±0.45). Participants performed 45% of the tasks moderately and 25% heavily; unloading bricks from the kiln top was the most dangerous according to the OWAS scale. Conclusion: Manual brick production entails heavy postural, thermal, and cardiovascular stress along with extremely high levels of musculoskeletal symptoms in female juveniles. There is an urgent need for intervention measures regarding ergonomics, nutrition, regulation, and education, including the abolition of hazardous juvenile labor, mechanization of load carrying, load restriction, rest breaks, hydration, safe postures, and schooling.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine educators’ perceptions of the ethical boundaries for using artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and academic assessment, distinguishing AI support from AI delegation using flipped learning as a pedagogical lens. Design/methodology/approach A questionnaire was administered to 148 faculty members from Universidade Autónoma de Lisboa, Portugal. The paper adopts an exploratory quantitative case-study design. Analysis used descriptive statistics, normalized Shannon entropy, Pearson correlation and a paired-samples t-test. Findings Respondents were open to AI support for routine, preparatory and lower-order learning activities, but more cautious when AI was associated with evaluation, fairness, interpretation and assessment decisions. Teacher judgment was strongly prioritized, while trust in AI-generated fair and unbiased evaluation remained limited. Entropy analysis showed relatively clear boundaries around AI bias and human judgment, but more contested boundaries around AI-supported evaluation, learner independence and critical reflection. Research limitations/implications The single-institution convenience sample should be interpreted as exploratory and analytically transferable rather than statistically generalizable. Practical implications Institutions should clarify where AI may support assessment and where human evaluative authority must remain explicit. Social implications The findings highlight the need for shared institutional norms. Originality/value The paper proposes the dual approach as an interpretive framework connecting ethical responsibility, cognitive complexity and flipped learning to distinguish AI support from delegated evaluative authority. Its contribution lies in locating the ethical boundary at the transfer of assessment responsibility and identifying where educators’ perceptions indicate crisp or fuzzy boundaries.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: It is assumed that the synergies created by the 6G communication technologies, blockchain organizations, and smart healthcare systems will introduce Society 5.0 in the form of the hyper-connected and patient-centric secure health ecosystem. These technologies are expected to provide an opportunity of unprecedented socio-economic value by real-time remote health monitoring and interaction, decentralized patient data management systems, and clinical decision making based on artificial intelligence. It is not only an ethical and societal but also a legal and regulatory challenge. Patient privacy, ownership of data, bias in the algorithm, and cyber security will have to be taken into consideration before we go into full deployment. Also, there exists no unified legal framework, as well as there are cross-border regulations to back a blockchain empowered contributor-led 6G healthcare system. The chapter will discuss ethical implications, legal issues, and regulations involved with 6G and blockchain-enabled health care and answer the question of what patients should think about informed consent when offered AI-led care, liability when making independent choices, and what the compliance with the right of the citizens to privacy under the jurisdiction of their nation (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), and what regulatory models might be available to decentralized health systems. We finally make high level recommendation concerning future policies and regulation to strike a balance between innovation, patient safety and social trust by the people.

As AI coding agents become integral to software development, projects increasingly utilise configuration files, such as context files and skills, to govern agent behaviour. While AI ethics principles are widely used in research and policy, little is known about whether and how they are reflected when developers configure coding agents. We studied ethics principles in 40,079 configuration files across 8,893 GitHub repositories. Using a validated large language model (LLM) classification, we measured the prevalence of ethics-related statements, and qualitatively analysed 702 stratified samples across 679 files to uncover the ethical considerations reflected in these files and the parties they concern. Ethics-related statements appeared in 39.4% of files and 61.5% of repositories; concentrated on accountability, transparency, privacy protection, and reliability; and occurred more often in task-specific files such as skills than in project-wide context files. Our qualitative analysis identified 30 categories of ethical considerations, which take the form of concrete rules for the agent. Accountability appeared mainly as requirements for human approval, transparency as explain and honestly report the agent's work, and fairness as accessibility and localisation. These considerations reveal a difference in focus. Whereas public ethics frameworks aim to protect society and end users, configuration files mainly concern developers, maintainers, and community members in the development workflow. Ethics-related content appeared mainly in prose-based files, and whether agents follow these instructions remains untested. We discuss the implications for practitioners, researchers, and policymakers.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been investigated for clinical documentation, with concerns about hallucinations and factual errors. Clinician review and revision of LLM-generated drafts are considered essential; however, the impact of such a workflow on both documentation time and quality remains unknown. This single-center, parallel-group, prospective, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint (PROBE) pilot trial evaluated whether a clinician-in-the-loop workflow improves clinical documentation time and quality compared with clinician-only drafting. From February 18 to March 14, 2025, at the Department of Ophthalmology, Kyoto University Hospital, 21 physicians were randomized, and 17 completed the intervention. Participants were randomized to either the Clinician-in-the-loop group or the Clinician-only group. Participants created discharge summaries and referrals for six simulated patient records. The Clinician-in-the-loop group reviewed and edited LLM-generated drafts, whereas the Clinician-only group drafted documents from scratch using matched templates. Unedited LLM drafts formed the LLM-only group. Seventeen physicians submitted 48 discharge summaries and 48 discharge referrals in the Clinician-in-the-loop group, 54 of each document type in the Clinician-only group, and 48 of each in the LLM-only group. Clinician-in-the-loop showed a shorter creation time for summaries (β = −59.4 seconds; 95% CI, −150.6 to 31.7; P = .18) and a longer creation time for referrals (β = 52.9 seconds; 95% CI, −7.0 to 112.9; P = .08) than Clinician-only, although neither difference was statistically significant. In most expert-rated quality domains, the clinician-in-the-loop workflow outperformed clinician-only drafting. LLM-only drafts were fastest but had the lowest quality. In conclusion, a clinician-in-the-loop approach generally improved document quality and, although the primary analysis showed no statistically significant difference in documentation time, suggested potential time savings for certain document types. These findings highlight the importance of active clinician supervision and support further evaluation of clinician-in-the-loop workflows in real-world clinical settings. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT07187050 (registered on September 18, 2025).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: A prevailing belief in quantitative finance is that deploying high-capacity foundation models inevitably generates superior predictive edge (Gu, Kelly, & Xiu, 2020). This paper presents an empirical evaluation testing whether zero-shot foundation forecasting (Google TimesFM 1.0-200M; Das, Kong, Sen, & Zhou, 2024) and kinematic derivatives physics enhance strike selection and compounding in systematic options selling across Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOG), and NVIDIA (NVDA) over a continuous 10-year cycle (October 2016 to October 2026 | 2,512 trading days), strictly partitioned into a 5-year In-Sample calibration epoch and a 5-year Out-of-Sample holdout period. We simulate mechanical options compounding under an idealized Zero-VRP invariant (pricing all contracts at zero implied-volatility premium via analytical Black-Scholes-Merton) to isolate pure directional and timing alpha from structural volatility premium capture. On this invariant benchmark, baseline rule-based mechanics achieve terminal equity of $2,349,600 on AMZN (23.50x), $821,300 on GOOG (8.21x), and $27,998,700 on NVDA (280.0x). Integrating TimesFM 10-day ahead forecasts to write defensive call overlays produces zero statistically detectable forecast edge: directional accuracy is indistinguishable from coin flips (50.8% AMZN, 51.2% GOOG, 49.8% NVDA; Diebold-Mariano p-values 0.27, 0.11, 0.42), while call truncation inflicts catastrophic opportunity cost on explosive trend legs (NVDA terminal wealth collapses from 280.0x to 10.9x). Furthermore, kinematic dip-buying rules (velocity-acceleration phase triggers) display severe parameter decay out of sample: on AMZN, out-of-sample terminal wealth sits at the 72.4th percentile of an uninformed random-put placebo (p = 0.28). Deflated Sharpe Ratios (DSR; Bailey & Lopez de Prado, 2014) across all evaluated machine learning enhancements fall to 0.00, demonstrating that the observed historical outperformance was a product of selection bias across non-stationary market regimes.

Predictive world models can simulate plausible future physical scenes, but their value as frozen representations for specialized industrial safety tasks remains unclear. We examine whether predictive future latents from NVIDIA Cosmos Predict2.5 2B add sample-specific information beyond a compact kinematic history for long-horizon forklift–worker risk forecasting. From a 2 s state history, the task predicts both agents’ positions, their cumulative minimum separation, and HIGH/WARNING/SAFE risk from +1 to +6 s. Using 1180 samples from 854 synthetic warehouse runs, a state-only predictor is compared with a residual fusion of aligned Cosmos latents, the same residual with shuffled latents, and a Cosmos-only model. On 300 test samples from 129 runs, the state-only model achieves a worker average displacement error of 0.484 m and a mean risk Macro-F1 of 0.846; the aligned residual yields 0.496 m and 0.845, and the shuffled control 0.485 m and 0.850. Run-level cluster bootstrap analysis and ten strict shuffled controls show no consistent alignment-specific benefit, and this conclusion holds under alternative risk thresholds and spatially preserving latent probes. The latent contains weak scene information that is largely redundant with the metric state. Matched state baselines and sample-correspondence controls are essential for evaluating foundation-model representations for physical-safety tasks.

This study aims to evaluate the implementation of digital Arabic language learning among students enrolled in an Arabic Language Education Study Program at a state university in Makassar, Indonesia, using the Context, Input, Process, and Product (CIPP) evaluation model. This study employed a qualitative evaluative approach, with the head of the study program, lecturers, and students participating as research participants. Data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews, and document analysis. The data were analyzed using the interactive model developed by Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña, comprising data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that, in the context dimension, the implementation of digital Arabic language learning aligns with the needs of digital transformation and the demands of twenty-first-century education. In the input dimension, digital infrastructure, institutional support, and lecturers’ competencies were generally adequate, although variations in students’ digital literacy remained evident. In the process dimension, digital learning facilitated student interaction, participation, and flexibility in learning. In the product dimension, the implementation contributed to improvements in Arabic language proficiency, learner autonomy, and students’ digital literacy. Overall, the findings indicate that the implementation of digital Arabic language learning was generally effective and warrants further development. This study recommends strengthening technological infrastructure, providing continuous digital literacy training, and optimizing the integration of digital technologies and artificial intelligence into Arabic language learning.

Abstract Mechanistic models, expressed as simulations that can be run and visualised, are a powerful way to understand biological and other systems. Building them, however, requires formulating mathematical or rule‐based descriptions and translating them into working code, skills that many ecologists and other disciplinary researchers do not have. Generative AI can now perform much of this translation, making mechanistic modelling accessible to researchers, educators and students previously excluded by its technical demands. But delegating this translation to AI also carries real risks: modelling assumptions can become hidden, plausible but incorrect code can pass unnoticed, and the skills and critical habits that model building once developed may never form. We examine the benefits and risks of using generative AI as a modelling companion at each stage of model development (conceptual specification, formalisation, implementation and exploration), drawing on recent experimental evidence on AI‐assisted learning and on a worked predator–prey example built with AI, with a rule‐based epidemic model as a parallel case. At each stage we identify where consequential decisions are silently delegated to the AI and set out practical mitigations that keep human judgement engaged without requiring the technical skills AI has made optional: specifying the conceptual model explicitly before engaging AI, having the AI translate its formalisation back into plain language, testing the implementation against outcomes known from domain knowledge and designing the interface to support interrogation. This new opportunity is substantial: researchers, educators and students who understand their systems but have never been able to build models of them are now able to explore these systems mechanistically, testing how components interact and how the system responds to conditions it has not yet experienced, questions that correlative approaches alone cannot answer. Used carelessly, AI risks eroding modelling skill for little lasting benefit, but used deliberately, in the ways set out here, it opens a new pathway to mechanistic understanding without removing the critical thinking the old technical barrier once enforced.

documents.abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide reliable external knowledge for multi-hop factual reasoning with large language models (LLMs), yet most KGs in real-world domains such as finance and industry lack question--answer (QA) annotations. Without such annotations, existing methods struggle to improve LLM graph reasoning: training-free agents cannot improve their exploration through interaction; reinforcement learning (RL) agents depend on QA data annotated by humans or synthesized by closed-source models; and training data is typically built offline, so its topology mix is fixed and cannot follow the agent's ability. We propose Evolve on Graph (EoG), a framework that lets an LLM self-evolve its graph reasoning without any QA annotations. Through Graph Self-Play, a single LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. To make questions verifiable, Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) samples reasoning topologies on the KG and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, yielding topology skeletons with correct and complete answer sets; guided by a skeleton, the Proposer explores the graph to pose a multi-hop question. To let task topologies follow the Solver, a Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum rewards the Proposer by the Solver's score variance, keeping questions at the Solver's capability boundary so that complex topologies enter training as the Solver improves. On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata, and an industrial KG, EoG consistently outperforms prompting-, retrieval-, and agent-based methods, showing that LLM graph reasoning can improve through self-play without QA annotations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Szy5/EoG

Serving web queries at scale with multi-agent systems requires jointly configuring large language models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills. However, the resulting configuration space grows combinatorially, while sparse execution rewards provide limited fine-grained supervision for interdependent planning decisions. We propose EvoRouter, a self-evolving multi-agent routing framework driven by insight-guided on-policy distillation. A dedicated expert periodically synthesizes performance-cost feedback from configuration trajectories across tasks into reusable conditional routing insights about capability requirements, returns from resource scaling, and interactions among configuration choices. A privileged teacher combines these evolving insights with current execution feedback to provide dense token-level supervision for the router's own planning trajectories through on-policy distillation. Cost-aware reinforcement learning jointly optimizes task performance and computational cost. Together, these training signals internalize execution insights into the routing policy. The updated policy generates new trajectories that support subsequent insight extraction, forming an execution-driven self-improvement loop. We evaluate EvoRouter on 19 in-domain datasets spanning five domains and two out-of-domain benchmarks. EvoRouter achieves an average in-domain accuracy of 68.69%, outperforming the strongest routing baseline by 7.23 percentage points while reducing inference compute cost by 50.95%. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/CenYangtze/EvoRouter.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming public health decision-making, shifting it from descriptive epidemiological reporting to predictive, accelerated operational guidance. Yet AI in public health is discussed almost entirely at technical or regulatory levels, leaving a gap in executive-level guidance. Public health operates within a complex landscape of social determinants, political scrutiny, and incomplete information, where algorithmic errors can severely damage public trust. Consequently, executive competency must expand beyond traditional data interpretation to foundational AI literacy. Leaders must differentiate among diverse AI applications and evaluate their risk profiles, including balancing AI trained on individual-level precision medicine models with public health population-level prevention mandate. Continuous human oversight and multidisciplinary validation should be standard for modern public health organizations. Automated systems must equitably advance population health outcomes under final human authority at all times. Public health executives can better prepare to make informed decisions about AI-related risks using the decision points presented in this commentary.

documents.abstract: In this study, three software reliability tasks are considered: predicting defect prone modules, software incidents severity classification, and predicting deployment change failures, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is studied for those tasks. For four explicitly synthetic tabular datasets with 2,400 data points each, that is, 7,200 observations, four classifiers were tested: logistic regression, random forest, extremely randomized trees and histogram gradient boosting. We were able to generate 12 model task evaluations, with 600 instances left out for each task. The accuracy and the macro-F1 scores of logistic regression were 77.17% and 75.40% for defect prediction, 72.00% and 72.33% for incident severity classification, and 64.33% and 63.69% for change-failure prediction, respectively. There are three areas of examination in the evaluation: predictive performance analysis, error patterns analysis, and model interpretation analysis. The confusion matrix, the receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and the balanced accuracy are all used to explore these areas, along with the Matthews correlation coefficient and the feature-importance analysis. Twenty publications on the topic are critically examined and used to put the benchmark into the context and its methodological choices. The study offers an evaluation protocol that conveys the explanation in terms that the reader can follow and a comparative simulation framework of three software engineering decision points, along with a discussion of the constraints of the shown tasks when it comes to deployment. It does not develop a new learning algorithm but rather it is methodological and comparative. The results reported here are only applicable to the data sets generated and external validity has not been established. Conclusions regarding the practical effectiveness and suitability to deployment of the operational software data should be based on an independent evaluation prior to their use.

documents.abstract: This study aims to investigate scholars’ and researchers’ perceptions, attitudes, and intentions toward using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic research. Employing a cross-sectional survey, data were collected from 1,283 participants in China. After removing missing values, 1150 valid responses were analyzed. Results indicate that perceived usefulness of GenAI was positively associated with attitudes (β = 0.489, p < 0.001) and directly associated with usage intention (β = 0.385, p < 0.001). Furthermore, attitudes toward GenAI had a positive effect on usage intention (β = 0.323, p < 0.001) and mediated the association between perceived usefulness and intention (indirect effect = 0.157, Boot95% CI [0.120, 0.199]). These findings underscore that positive perceptions of GenAI’s usefulness are associated with more favorable attitudes and stronger intentions to adopt it in research. By applying the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to GenAI adoption, this study highlights the need for academic institutions to promote responsible use through ethical guidelines, training programs, and awareness campaigns, which may facilitate effective integration into research practices.

Abstract Objective: Chagas disease remains an important public health problem, particularly in Latin America, where chronic infection frequently leads to cardiac involvement and associated structural changes. Recent advances in deep learning (DL) have enabled automated image analysis of chest X-ray (CXR) in several clinical applications, yet little is known about its applicability to Chagas disease. However, the potential of these methods for Chagas disease screening remains largely unexplored. Approach: In this study, we investigate the feasibility of DL models to identify patients with Chagas disease from CXR images. A private dataset of CXRs was used to train and evaluate several convolutional neural network architectures. Main results: Among the evaluated models, EfficientNet-B4 achieved the best overall performance metrics, with accuracy of 0.655 ± 0.026, precision of 0.653 ± 0.041, recall of 0.700 ± 0.157, F1-score of 0.664 ± 0.076, and AUC of 0.727 ± 0.015. Significance: These results indicate that CXRs contain subtle imaging features associated with chronic Chagas disease that can be partially captured by DL models, although the overall discriminative performance remains moderate. While CXR-based DL models are unlikely to serve as a standalone diagnostic tool, they may have potential as complementary screening or triage tools, particularly in settings where chest radiographs are routinely acquired and access to specialized diagnostic testing is limited.. These findings highlight both the feasibility and the limitations of applying artificial intelligence to support Chagas disease screening using routinely acquired radiographic images.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Intelligent automation has gained relevance in business management because of its ability to optimize processes, improve information, and support decision-making. However, there is limited evidence on the organizational conditions that may modify its relationship with financial decisions in Peruvian MSEs. Methods A quantitative, applied, non-experimental, and cross-sectional study was conducted with 372 managers of service MSEs in Chiclayo, selected through simple random sampling. A 36-item questionnaire with a five-category Likert scale was administered, and descriptive analyses, Spearman correlations, and moderated regression with centered variables and HC3 robust errors were used, complemented by slopes and the Johnson-Neyman procedure. Results Intelligent automation was positively and significantly associated with financial decisions (B = .404; p < .001) and explained 28.5% of their variability. The global interactions with digitalization and managerial experience were not individually significant, although their joint evaluation was significant (p = .045). In the dimensional model, only the interaction trust in results × digitalization was significant (B = .120; p = .009). Conclusions Intelligent automation was favorably related to financial decisions, especially in firms with higher levels of digitalization.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Expert advice on crop management is often written informally, and in such text a number can easily be assigned the wrong role or attached to the wrong operation, material, or measurement basis. We propose QS-IE, a knowledge extraction method constrained by quantity and operation scope. Its unit of extraction is a complete quantitative fact. Given a shared set of numeric candidates and a single base model, QS-IE selects complete candidates from several prompting strategies, verifies them against the source text, and applies scope constraints, so that every extracted quantity stays linked to its source evidence. We built a corpus of 4006 texts on tomato cultivation. Two researchers with agronomy backgrounds jointly annotated and reviewed 1000 of them; the other 3006 were annotated with large language model assistance and then reviewed by hand. The corpus was split into 3206 development texts and 800 independent test texts. On the 1152 reference facts of the test set, QS-IE reached a precision of 84.02%, a recall of 86.72%, and a micro-averaged F1 of 85.35%, which is 3.91 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, a multi-strategy in-context learning ensemble. Removing the operation scope constraints lowered test F1 by 8.24 percentage points. In a sampled human audit of the test set, 82.00% of the outputs for texts containing target facts were judged usable, and all six engineering checks on storage and evidence traceability were passed. The results indicate that explicit association constraints make quantitative facts extracted from tomato cultivation texts more complete and easier to review, which supports the structured, traceable storage of experiential knowledge that experts express in non-standardized text.

Abstract Extrusion technology has emerged as one of the most versatile processing methods for developing functional foods from Andean grains, responding to the increasing global demand for nutritious, sustainable, and gluten-free products. This review critically examines recent advances in the extrusion processing of quinoa, kiwicha, and kañiwa, with emphasis on the interactions between raw material composition, thermomechanical processing parameters, and final product functionality. The review discusses the influence of formulation strategies, extrusion conditions, and specific mechanical energy on starch gelatinisation, protein texturisation, expansion behaviour, and bioactive compound retention. Furthermore, it evaluates the application of conventional and emerging approaches, including high-moisture extrusion, artificial intelligence-based process optimisation, machine learning, and Industry 4.0 technologies, to improve process control and product quality. Current evidence demonstrates that the synergistic integration of ingredient design, extrusion engineering, and predictive modelling is essential for maximising nutritional value, technological performance, and industrial scalability. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on extrusion conditions or grain composition independently, this study presents an integrated techno-functional framework linking formulation strategies, extrusion parameters, nutritional outcomes, and industrial applications. This framework identifies key interactions and research gaps to support the rational design of next-generation extruded foods with enhanced functionality, improved nutritional quality, and sustainable commercial competitiveness.

Large language models are increasingly used to turn the feature attributions of multimodal prognostic models into narratives for clinicians, yet costly modalities such as amyloid PET and cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers are often missing, and whether these explanations stay faithful under missing evidence has not been tested. We separate two failure points: phantom attribution, in which the model credits modalities that were never observed, and unfaithful narration, in which the report omits, cites or misjudges missing modalities. Using 307 participants of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative with complete data, we masked every subset of four costly modalities, predicted 36-month conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease, and restored the masked data to obtain interventional ground truth. All five missing-data strategies assigned 12% to 23% of attribution to unobserved modalities, and up to 45% with four absent; missingness-aware strategies minimised it at no cost in accuracy. Across 51,200 reports from four language models and four prompting regimes, naming absent modalities in the prompt raised acknowledgement from 48% to 88% and cut phantom evidence twenty-fold, but advice on whether acquiring a missing test would change the prediction was correct in only 27% to 41% of cases until checked against executed restorations, which raised accuracy to 69% for open-weight narrators and 99.9% for a proprietary model. Higher phantom attribution was associated with more phantom evidence and fewer faithful direction claims, and direction fidelity, measured by a calibrated language-model judge, depended on narrator scale rather than prompting. Narrators told to name absent modalities sometimes declared observed ones absent, an error that a structured template eliminated. We release the masking protocol and evaluation code.

Controlling personality in large language models is important for building conversational agents that can be customized to different users and interaction settings. However, existing personality control methods often face a tradeoff between strong trait expression and natural dialogue generation. We introduce FATE-5, Faithful Alignment of Trait Expression for the Big Five, a two-stage framework that separates personality encoding from naturalness alignment. FATE-5 first learns continuous soft prompt representations of Big Five profiles using dialogue supervision and an auxiliary survey objective. It then improves dialogue naturalness through preference alignment based on both dialogue quality and personality agreement. Across three language model backbones, FATE-5 maintains strong trait expression while achieving substantially higher dialogue naturalness than other trait-strong methods. On held-out questionnaires, it achieves monotonicity correlations of 0.97-0.99 and recovery RMSE of 8.9-12.4, substantially improving over the evaluated baselines. These results demonstrate effective continuous personality control while maintaining natural conversational behavior.

Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.

Continuous Integration and Delivery (CI/CD) are fundamental to modern software development, yet configuring pipelines such as GitHub Actions (GHA) workflows remains complex and error-prone. Recent work has explored Transformer-based models for GHA workflow recommendation, but existing approaches typically model workflow steps as a single homogeneous generation task. This formulation overlooks a key distinction: reusable Actions are structured, ecosystem-level components, whereas project-specific Scripts encode local build, test, and deployment semantics. Consequently, current models struggle to capture the different forms of knowledge required for accurate workflow completion. In this work, we present FLOWSTEP, a framework for GHA workflow step completion that explicitly distinguishes between Action and Script generation. FLOWSTEP combines large language models (LLMs) with contrastive learning to better capture semantic relationships among workflow contexts, Actions, and Scripts. Evaluated on established benchmarks, FLOWSTEP improves end-to-end workflow step prediction accuracy from 38.23% to 51.09%. Beyond prediction accuracy, we further study whether LLM-as-a-judge can provide a more semantic evaluation of generated workflow steps. By comparing LLM-based assessments with human annotations, we find that the best-performing model configuration reaches substantial agreement with human ground truth (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.701), suggesting that LLM-as-a-judge can serve as a scalable complement to manual evaluation.

Forensic intelligence (FORINT) is a powerful extension of forensic science's role in policing and security, enabling forward-leaning forensic contributions for wider effect, including prevention and disruption of crime. However, operational implementation has been inhibited by concerns relating to quality and the potential for misinterpretation or misuse of forensic information. To directly apply laboratory-centric quality assurance approaches to FORINT would be to place it in a Procrustean bed, ill-suited to its transdisciplinary, adaptive, and often predictive approach to generating activity/crime level propositions and other insights. However, FORINT can, and should, be delivered within a principles-based quality management framework, wherein quality is a property of the system – not a restrictive compliance mechanism. Through established quality system principles, intelligence theory and forensic science, and extensive operational experience, a structured FORINT delivery framework is proposed, leveraging recognised constructs such as the ‘intelligence cycle’ and FORINT praxis with standards familiar to forensic scientists, without imposing rigid, laboratory-focused requirements. Quality considerations are mapped to structured processes across planning, collection, collation, analysis, review & reporting, and dissemination & evaluation. Focus is accorded to leadership, customer/decision-maker engagement, workforce design, and governance. Human factors are recognised throughout, as FORINT analysis involves contextualised interpretation and judgement of complex, incomplete, and uncertain information under pressure. The model is structured to mitigate bias and misinterpretation, ensuring ethical, reliable, and defensible assessments. These recommendations position FORINT as an effective, robust means of maximising the utility of scientific insights, enhancing the outcomes of forensic science and policing intelligence, while maintaining the trust of practitioners, decision-makers, and the public.

Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces (LTLf) is widely used in Artificial Intelligence to specify desired temporal behavior and determine whether finite traces satisfy or violate it. Explaining these outcomes is essential for debugging and trust. However, existing approaches typically capture either sufficient reasons or counterfactual causes, without clarifying their relationship. We introduce a native characterization of abductive (AXps) and contrastive (CXps) explanations directly over finite traces, based on locking and unlocking time-indexed events. We prove its equivalence to the classifier-based formulation, and show that CXps coincide with a recently proposed temporal causality semantics for LTLf. This characterization enables an efficient implementation based on the enumeration of minimal unsatisfiable cores and minimal correction sets of ASP programs. Experiments on real-world event logs demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

documents.abstract: This study explores how undergraduate Generation Z students at an international college in Thailand adopt and use AI chatbots. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a sensitizing framework, we conducted an exploratory convergent mixed-methods survey of 144 eligible students. Quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics and exploratory factor analysis of seven adoption items adapted from TAM and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), while qualitative analysis used LLM-assisted, researcher-verified coding of 127 and 117 substantive open-ended responses to examine motivations and desired features. The analysis suggested two provisional adoption-related dimensions, perceived relational value and social endorsement, and practical accessibility, although the factor-retention criteria were divided between one and two factors. Almost all students selected academic assistance as a reason for using AI chatbots (92.4%). Asked specifically about AI companions, students most often cited information seeking and convenience (27.6% of substantive responses), while personal and emotional support and reservations about companion use were raised in 20.5% and 19.7% of responses, respectively. Human-like interaction was the most frequently requested feature category (39.3%), followed by technical capabilities and academic tools such as citation support. The study contributes exploratory, cross-sectional evidence on AI chatbot adoption in a Thai higher-education context and highlights the importance of balancing practical utility, relational expectations, and clear human-AI boundaries.

ABSTRACT The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into academic writing has raised ethical questions about intellectual property, authorship, and knowledge representation. Although existing research has examined academic integrity and AI literacy, how learners negotiate responsibility when responding to biased or culturally inappropriate AI‐generated outputs remains underexplored. Grounded in critical applied linguistics and informed by relational accountability and distributed agency, this study examines how students enacted accountability in an AI bias analysis task within an undergraduate English academic writing course at a Chinese university. Drawing on group reports, AI interaction records, reflective writing, field notes, and interviews, thematic analysis identified three interrelated orientations through which students enacted accountability: epistemic accountability (evaluating knowledge claims), relational accountability (negotiating responsibility across human‐AI relations), and ecological accountability (questioning the broader linguistic, cultural, and epistemic consequences of AI‐generated knowledge). These orientations reveal accountability as distributed across epistemic judgments, social and technological relations, and broader conditions of knowledge representation. We conceptualize this configuration as distributed accountability: a situated process through which learners negotiate and enact answerability for AI‐mediated knowledge and its consequences. By demonstrating this expansion of answerability, the study connects the micro‐ethics of classroom practice with the macro‐ethics of linguistic and epistemic diversity and equity in AI‐mediated knowledge production. It offers implications for future research on academic writing ethics, critical AI literacy, and educational AI governance in applied linguistics.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Faculty development programmes must adapt to changing expectations in curriculum design, assessment, educational scholarship, technology, leadership and interprofessional practice. The Diploma in Medical Education (Dip. Med. Ed.) at the Defence Services Medical Academy (DSMA), Myanmar, provides a longitudinal example of such adaptation. In 2024, DSMA and the Military Institute of Nursing and Paramedical Sciences (MINP) combined their contributions to the programme, marking a new collaborative phase in its development. This study examined how the DSMA Dip. Med. Ed. programme changed between 2010 and 2026 and to identify the principal curricular and institutional transitions that moved it from foundational faculty development toward contemporary health professions education, including the development of DSMA-MINP collaboration from 2024. We conducted a retrospective documentary analysis using course handbooks from the first course in 2010-2011 through the 16th course handbook in 2026. A structured extraction framework examined programme aims, duration, curriculum architecture, teaching-learning strategies, educational technology, assessment, leadership, communication and professionalism, educational research, workshops and governance. The authors compared documents chronologically and synthesized recurring patterns and material changes into developmental phases. Five phases were identified: foundation and formalisation (2010-2013); consolidation of the modular faculty-development model (2014-2019); outcomes, constructive alignment and digitally supported delivery (2020-2023); DSMA-MINP collaboration and curricular expansion (2024-2025); and further curriculum modernisation (2026). The 2026 curriculum incorporated outcome-based and competency-based medical education, curriculum mapping, quality assurance and accreditation, interprofessional education, problem- and case-based learning, e-learning, simulation, artificial intelligence and AI ethics, educational governance, professionalism, research ethics and critical appraisal. The Dip. Med. Ed. retained a stable core mission while progressively broadening from teacher preparation to a more integrated health professions education programme. The combination of DSMA and MINP from 2024 and the subsequent curricular developments through 2026 represent important milestones in this transformation. Future evaluation should determine whether these intended curriculum changes translate into sustained changes in educational practice, scholarship and institutional outcomes.

The development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications has profound implications for higher education,including student behaviors, engagement, and productivity in learning. While academic literature addressing the implications of AI applications is on the rise, its relevance for fields of economics, business,and the social sciences remains disparate and localized. In this regard, this paper analyzes the bibliometric landscape of AI research using a set of indicators that include keyword co-occurrence, time and research density, and emerging research fronts using VOSviewer, and the search was limited to Scopus-indexed journal articles (2000-2025).A descriptive analysis was done based on three sets of documents, namely the global baseline, the discipline-specific body of work,and a local Malaysian dataset. The global dataset has produced a mature and integrated network with a primary emphasis on educational data mining and learning analytics.Nevertheless, temporal overlay visualization analysis reveals a sharp transition to the human and ethical factors surrounding generative artificial intelligence, including academic integrity and frameworks for evaluating teacher acceptance of disruptive technologies. In contrast, the Malaysian dataset was found to have a sparsely connected network, suggesting the growing nature of local research. Indeed, studies pertaining to Malaysia appear to focus on the interactions between students and ChatGPT and lack psychological theories in any of the included works.This study has identified the fundamental disconnect between regional and international research practices.As such, it can serve as the foundation for future studies that seek to understand the effects of artificial intelligence on the emotional,social, and academic development of students in developed digital economies.

Cervical cancer is a major global health challenge, especially in low- and middle-income countries, despite the availability of effective prophylactic human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines, screening methods and established treatments. Cervical cancer is primarily caused by persistent infection with high-risk HPV, but persistent infection is necessary, but not sufficient, for the development of cancer. Advances in understanding HPV genetic diversity, viral persistence, and virus-host molecular interactions are creating new opportunities to improve precision in HPV prevention and treatment. HPV genotype distribution and differences in oncogenic potential inform vaccine development and screening strategies. The viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 disrupt host tumor-suppressor pathways, driving cellular immortalization and genomic instability. Molecular events such as viral insertion, epigenetic modifications, APOBEC-associated mutations, and immune escape contribute to disease progression. These discoveries have revealed molecular vulnerabilities that can be targeted therapeutically. Immune checkpoint inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates are used clinically in specific contexts of cervical cancer presentation and treatment. At the same time, therapeutic vaccines, adoptive cellular immunotherapies, RNA interference, and genome editing are being investigated as complementary strategies to target HPV-associated cervical cancer. With advances in next-generation sequencing, molecular biomarkers, and artificial intelligence, these tools could further refine risk stratification and therapy selection. This review explores the current understanding of HPV genetic variation and virus-host interactions driving a shift from traditional prevention and treatment strategies to precision prevention and targeted therapeutics, and critically assesses remaining challenges.

This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.

Many enterprise generative AI initiatives stall between a successful pilot and dependable production use. Industry forecasts suggest that at least 30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept, and that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. This paper argues that the gap is primarily a management and delivery problem rather than a model-capability problem, and proposes a practitioner framework for go-live decisions. The framework rests on a single organizing analogy, treating an AI system like a new hire, and translates it into seven readiness checks (value, ownership, data, evaluation, guardrails, operations and adoption), six hard stops that block launch regardless of overall score, an eight-part evidence pack, a 0–2 scoring rubric, and an additional control set for agentic systems that can take actions. The checks are mapped to established sources including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, and empirical work on machine learning engineering. Seven publicly documented cases are used to illustrate the failure modes each check is designed to catch. The paper closes with limitations and a proposed agenda for empirical validation. JEL classification: M15, O32, O33.

documents.abstract: For large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), model-reported self-confidence is often miscalibrated, yet it may still be useful for efficient evaluation. At the same time, LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to direct human auditing, but its practical benefit depends on calibration quality and inference cost. This paper develops a unified statistical framework for both evaluation routes under alternative sampling strategies. For direct auditing, confidence-stratified sampling is used to recover population accuracy from partially verified outputs without requiring calibrated confidence. Finite-sample uncertainty is characterized, and the analysis shows how highly uneven confidence strata affect audit efficiency and label allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, the judge is modeled through sensitivity and false-positive rate, yielding an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty. The two routes are then compared through human-label and total-cost efficiency boundaries. Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro show that miscalibrated self-confidence can still support statistically valid stratified auditing. Under highly imbalanced confidence distributions, proportional allocation substantially reduces estimation error relative to equal-per-stratum allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, only a small subset of target--verifier pairs satisfies the idealized human-label efficiency condition, and automated inference costs can further limit potential savings. These findings clarify the statistical and economic conditions under which confidence-guided auditing and automated verification are useful.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping graduate employability by changing how competencies are enacted, valued, and developed. While traditional employability frameworks identify competencies expected of graduates, limited research has examined how these competencies may be evolving within AI-enabled environments. This study examines established employability competency domains and explores faculty perceptions of emerging capability requirements in the age of generative AI. A sequential mixed-method design was adopted. Quantitative data from 177 graduating business students in Saudi Arabia were analysed using domain-level principal component analysis to assess the internal structure and reliability of seven established competency domains. Semi-structured interviews with twelve business faculty members were subsequently analysed thematically. The quantitative findings provide context-specific support for communication, leadership, critical thinking and problem-solving, teamwork, management capability, ICT capability, and professionalism. The qualitative findings identified three complementary patterns of perceived competency evolution: human-centric enduring competencies, AI-augmented competencies, and emerging AI-specific competencies. The findings suggest that AI-ready employability involves both the continuing relevance of established competencies and changes in how competencies are enacted alongside intelligent technologies. The study proposes an exploratory AI-ready employability framework integrating established competencies with perceived competency continuity, augmentation, and emergence, providing a foundation for further empirical investigation and curriculum development in AI-integrated higher education.

In light of Large Language Models (LLMs), which are drastically altering creative environments, this chapter addresses Hybrid Human-AI Collaboration Models. LLMs provide previously unheard-of skills in data analysis, content creation with sophisticated reasoning, their successful application requires a sophisticated awareness of their drawbacks, such as their vulnerability to bias, factual inaccuracies, and a lack of practical experience. In order to bridge this gap, hybrid models create organized frameworks that integrate the unique advantages of artificial and human intelligence in a complementary way. In this chapter different collaborative architectures, with an emphasis on models that range from AI-driven workflows with human oversight (where LLM directs the process and a human provides crucial validation and ethical correction) to AI augmentation (where the human is the primary decision-maker and LLM serves as an assistant). The ‘human-in-the-loop’ mechanism is essential to these models because it ensures accountability, quality control, and the application of ethical judgment and contextual knowledge—all of which are now outside the purview of even the most sophisticated LLMs. Through case studies that highlight best practices for task decomposition, interaction design, and performance measurements, the chapter explores the real-world applications of these concepts in domains such as technical writing, software development, and strategic decision-making. At last, hybrid models are needed to minimize LLM risks and for enabling new steps of creativity and productivity, deciding the movement of human-computer interaction in the generative AI.

Many academic disciplines (in particular, mathematics and the theoretical sciences) face difficult questions about how to adapt their practices to the rise of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI). Before AI, a well-written research paper with a strong theoretical result acted as a reliable signal that its authors understood their field in depth. Now that AI is widely accessible, such signals have become cheaper to produce. As a result, they no longer reliably sort academics by their level of understanding. This has direct consequences for academic hiring. The age of AI raises a question for each side of the academic job market. Should an early-career researcher invest in a deep understanding of their field, or instead use AI to build a longer resume with many papers? Should a recruiter favor applicants with fewer papers who pass an interview aimed at probing understanding, or insist on both publication volume and a pass? In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model of this two-sided dilemma. We classify all pure-strategy equilibria that can arise in this game and use learning simulations to identify the behaviors that populations of applicants and recruiters may learn to adopt. Our analysis provides a framework for reasoning about how academic hiring can adapt to AI and for evaluating practices that preserve the value of deep understanding.

Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education (HE) worldwide, yet evidence from Asia remains limited. This study examines how students, teachers, and other stakeholders in Asia perceive the role of GenAI in HE, identifying current usage trends and analysing how GenAI is incorporated into academic and pedagogical practices. Using a mixed methods design, the study gathered quantitative data through online surveys of undergraduate students and teachers. Qualitative insights were obtained through focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews with a sample of participants, including policymakers, educationists, I/NGO representatives, and IT sector professionals. Findings show that the research participants hold mixed views about the role of GenAI in HE, with some indications of integration into academic practices. The study provides insights into emerging GenAI practices in Asian HE and highlights implications for policy and pedagogical development.
