documents.abstract: Research on coding agents mainly focuses on generation quality. Yet, safety-critical automotive software makes two additional demands. It prioritizes verification, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against industry standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR before it can be committed. It is also a narrow domain, written against layered architectures, embedded resource constraints, and organization-specific interface conventions that are scarce in the data general-purpose LLMs are trained on. We present a coding assistant for automotive C/C++ that addresses both demands. First, it exposes three tools to the user over the Model Context Protocol (generate, edit, and verify), allowing developers to run verify on any code on demand rather than relying on the agent to check its own output. Second, rather than using a general-purpose model, we customize the underlying LLM for the automotive domain through prompt engineering and fine-tuning. We construct a dataset from automotive production code of AUMOVIO, where each function is paired with the requirement texts and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior it must satisfy. In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers report verify as the most-used tool and confirm using it on their own code and not only on generated output. Comparing model customization strategies, 75% prefer the faster prompt-engineered configuration. MISRA- and AUTOSAR-inspired pattern checkers indicate that prompt engineering achieves a lower number of violations on C, while fine-tuning shows better conformance with architecture patterns for C++.

ABSTRACT The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in learning enables students to delegate some cognitive processes to technology, a practice known as cognitive offloading. Although this practice may improve efficiency, using AI without critical evaluation may contribute to an illusion of competence, defined as a discrepancy between perceived understanding and actual performance. This study examined the relationship between AI-based cognitive offloading and the illusion of competence, as well as the mediating role of critical thinking among high school students in Makassar. A quantitative cross-sectional correlational design and purposive sampling were employed, involving 356 students aged 15–18 years. Cognitive offloading was measured using an adapted Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking using the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, and the illusion of competence through the discrepancy between Judgment of Learning and performance on an objective PISA-based test. Data were analyzed using Confirmatory Factor Analysis and path analysis in Mplus 8.4. The CFA results indicated acceptable measurement models for cognitive offloading and critical thinking. Path analysis showed that cognitive offloading was positively associated with the illusion of competence and negatively associated with critical thinking, while critical thinking was negatively associated with the illusion of competence. The significant indirect effect indicated complementary partial mediation. These findings highlight the importance of analyzing, evaluating, and verifying AI-generated output to support accurate judgments of understanding. ABSTRAK Penggunaan artificial intelligence (AI) generatif dalam pembelajaran memungkinkan pelajar menyerahkan sebagian proses kognitif kepada teknologi atau melakukan cognitive offloading. Meskipun meningkatkan efisiensi, penggunaan tanpa evaluasi kritis dapat menimbulkan illusion of competence, yaitu ketidaksesuaian antara keyakinan terhadap pemahaman dan performa aktual. Penelitian ini bertujuan menguji hubungan cognitive offloading berbasis AI dengan illusion of competence serta peran mediasi critical thinking pada pelajar SMA di Kota Makassar. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain cross-sectional correlational dan purposive sampling, melibatkan 356 pelajar berusia 15–18 tahun. Cognitive offloading diukur menggunakan adaptasi Cognitive Outsourcing Behavior Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, critical thinking menggunakan Critical Thinking Disposition Scale for High School Students, sedangkan illusion of competence dioperasionalkan melalui ketidaksesuaian antara Judgment of Learning dan tes objektif berbasis PISA. Data dianalisis menggunakan Confirmatory Factor Analysis dan path analysis pada Mplus 8.4. Hasil CFA menunjukkan bahwa model pengukuran cognitive offloading dan critical thinking memiliki kesesuaian yang dapat diterima. Path analysis menunjukkan bahwa cognitive offloading berhubungan positif dengan illusion of competence dan negatif dengan critical thinking, sedangkan critical thinking berhubungan negatif dengan illusion of competence. Efek tidak langsung melalui critical thinking juga signifikan dan menunjukkan complementary partial mediation. Temuan ini menegaskan bahwa kemampuan menganalisis, mengevaluasi, dan memverifikasi keluaran AI merupakan bagian penting dalam menjaga ketepatan pelajar ketika menilai pemahamannya.

Generative AI has made plausible output abundant and cheap, but plausibility is not evidence and evidence is not authority. Leading AI assistants already concede this in the notice beneath every prompt box, telling users the system can make mistakes and asking them to check — handing the work of verification to individuals without instruments, records or authority. This working paper proposes Computational Trust Engineering (CTE), an engineering discipline for the path from a language model’s completion to an organization’s consequence. It separates three selections that current practice collapses into one: a generative selection (which continuation is probable?), an evidentiary selection (which candidate is supportable?) and an authority selection (may the supported candidate produce consequence?). CTE grounds these in four realities (human, AI, actual and governance reality) and treats familiar failure modes as measurable gaps between them. It frames evidentiary selection as metrology, with the individual claim as the counted unit, “unknown” as a legitimate result, calibrated instruments and traceable provenance. It introduces attention as the allocation of scarce measurement effort, and states when a language model may serve as an instrument. The paper defends the three-layer separation through collapse analysis and precedent from internal control, functional safety and metrology. It also maps CTE to the NIST AI RMF, NIST AI 600-1, ISO/IEC 42001, assurance cases and the EU AI Act, and closes with deployment postures, five falsifiable hypotheses and a research agenda.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explores how Generative AI has influenced research on AI literacy education at the elementary school level. A systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conducted to study implementations of Generative AI and methods of AI literacy education in elementary education. The review data includes 211 studies published from 2021 to January 2026 identified from SCOPUS, EBSCO, Web of Science, and Taylor & Francis. Thematic content analysis was used to identify and analyze themes in the review data to examine how the research field has developed after the release of Generative AI technology. The analysis identifies fundamental issues affecting the implementation of Generative AI in elementary education, including concerns about human interaction, varying approaches to ethical questions, and frequent concerns regarding the reliability of Generative AI outputs. The definition of the ethical dimensions of critical AI literacy is found to be inconclusive, calling for a broader adoption of critical AI literacy education at the elementary school level. Established use cases of Generative AI are identified, especially with self-regulated learning and foreign language studies. A holistic and integrated approach to AI literacy education for students and pre-service teachers is supported by the analysis. This study identifies research gaps for longitudinal research on Generative AI in elementary schools, parents’ role in students’ AI literacy, and a need to reach a scholarly consensus on the definition of AI ethics.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is widely expected to transform professional practices across multiple sectors, including the legal profession. This article critically examines the growing integration of GenAI tools into legal work and the implications this development carries for professional competence, ethical responsibility, and the broader institutional structure of legal practice. While AI promises substantial gains in efficiency by automating tasks such as legal research, document drafting, information retrieval, and data analysis, their adoption also raises significant concerns regarding reliability, transparency, confidentiality, and professional accountability. While prevailing narratives surrounding AI adoption in law often frame technological integration as both inevitable and normatively desirable, emphasising efficiency and competitive advantage while downplaying potential risks and value conflicts, the increasing delegation of professional tasks to algorithmic systems challenges traditional understandings of legal expertise, particularly in relation to judgement, reasoning, and professional autonomy. Moreover, unequal access to advanced AI tools and proprietary datasets may reinforce structural inequalities within the legal market, benefitting larger firms while disadvantaging smaller practices. This article argues for a balanced approach that combines technological literacy with strong ethical frameworks and institutional safeguards. Ultimately, responsible integration of GenAI requires sustained human oversight and collective professional engagement to ensure that technological innovation supports, rather than undermines, the core values of legal practice.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how knowledge-oriented generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tool use (GAIU) is associated with sports communication knowledge creation intention (SCKCI), with digital literacy (DL) and individual absorptive capacity (IAC) as sequential capability pathways. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 616 university students in Yunnan Province, China, with sport-related academic backgrounds or sports communication experience was analysed using confirmatory factor analysis, latent-variable structural equation modelling and 5,000 resample bootstrap mediation. Composite-score mediation served as a robustness check. Findings Both specific indirect paths and the sequential GAIU–DL–IAC–SCKCI path were significant, while the direct association remained significant, yielding a pattern consistent with partial sequential mediation. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, self-reported and region-specific design does not establish causal or temporal ordering and limits generalisability. SCKCI reflects intention rather than observed behaviour. Practical implications GenAI-supported knowledge work should incorporate source verification, human review and traceability. Social implications Responsible GenAI use in public-facing sports communication requires attention to misinformation, accountability and public trust. Originality/value This study conceptualises GenAI-mediated external knowledge input as generative yet epistemically uncertain and advances a verification-before-absorption logic that distinguishes the epistemic qualification of AI-generated information from its subsequent assimilation and transformation.

This chapter examines language-based generative AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), as active epistemic agents in leadership development. Moving beyond their perceived neutrality, the authors argue that LLMs serve as mirrors of dominant assumptions, co-constructors of leadership meaning, and framing devices of legitimate knowledge. The sources highlight how these systems reinforce prevailing Euro-American managerial ideals, often marginalizing diverse leadership paradigms such as Indigenous, collectivist, or spiritual frameworks, thereby amplifying structural and cultural biases. Through epistemic feedback loops and personalization, LLMs can subtly shape leadership identity and constrain developmental horizons, leading to adaptive standardization or performative conformity. The chapter emphasizes the critical need for epistemic responsibility in innovation leadership, advocating for leaders to interrogate system framings, reflect on their influence, and cultivate design awareness. This involves fostering inclusive data practices, participatory design methodologies, and culturally responsive AI governance to ensure AI-mediated innovation ecosystems are just, inclusive, and reflect pluralistic worldviews. Ultimately, the chapter calls for leaders to reclaim framing power and engage AI dialogically to foster an innovation leadership that is reflexive, ethically grounded, and attuned to human complexities.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This paper presents a generative AI-driven framework designed for e-commerce brand marketing, which integrates marketing content generation with user response prediction. By combining product information, brand characteristics, user behavior data, and contextual information, the framework generates semantically aligned marketing content and predicts user responses, such as click-through rates and purchase intentions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several baseline models in content generation and user response prediction tasks. The framework provides practical support for personalized marketing, content delivery, and decision-making. Moreover, it exhibits strong robustness under challenging scenarios, such as missing user data and content perturbation. This study highlights the potential of generative AI for optimizing both content creation and marketing performance in digital commerce environments.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how students retrieve and consume academic information, yet whether it substitutes for or complements library resources remains contested, and prior surveys rarely separate auxiliary from substitutive use. Methods This study uses a convergent triangulation design that combines multiple quantitative methods. It addresses the same set of research propositions by collecting perceptual-level questionnaire data and behavioral-level logs and platform usage statistics, analyzing them independently, and comparing the findings at the interpretation stage. Using 368 student questionnaires, we test an auxiliary-substitutive dual-path structural equation model and compare the results with an interrupted time-series analysis of 3.2 million print-loan logs (2017-2025) and digital-platform statistics from 2021 to the first half of 2026. Results Print-resource continuance intention is positively associated with deep-reading demand, but not significantly associated with auxiliary GenAI use. Survey results showed auxiliary GenAI use positively associated with digital-resource continuance intention, yet insufficiently distinct from perceived digital-resource convenience; platform data showed nascent use of embedded AI features. Substitutive GenAI use shows only a weak negative association with print-resource continuance intention, while the nine-year loan record reveals no significant level or trend change at the January 2023 breakpoint; task-channel fit shows no significant moderating effect. Discussion In this institution, findings align more with dual-channel coexistence than with the “AI-replaces-libraries” narrative; the survey-level substitution association has not yet appeared in aggregate borrowing behavior, informing collection development, service redesign, and AI-literacy education.
topics: Library Collection Development and Digital Resources

documents.abstract: Aim: To map recent artificial intelligence research in family medicine and primary care against an earlier 2015–2024 bibliometric baseline. Methods: Scopus was searched on 9 July 2026 for 2016–2026 publications. One researcher screened 3452 articles and reviews; 132 topical and 13 language exclusions left 3307 records. Manual title, DOI, and Scopus-identifier checks identified no duplicates. VOSviewer 1.6.21 and Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix 5.4.1; R 4.6.1) supported descriptive analysis and mapping. Results: Output increased from 531 in 2024 to 792 in 2025 (49.2%). The 2025 and partial 2026 component contained 1407 records (42.5%); 615 were dated 2026. The USA led publication and raw citation rankings (711 publications; 18,671 citations), while China preceded the United Kingdom in publication count. The Journal of Medical Internet Research (78 publications) and Scientific Reports (69) led the venues; seven top ten venues were shared with the earlier study. Language model terminology coexisted with later-positioned explainability, risk stratification, and diagnostic accuracy terms. Conclusions: This updated map quantifies post-2024 activity and identifies continuity and corpus-dependent differences in geography, dissemination, and evaluation-related vocabulary. Single-database and English language coverage, single-researcher screening, unadjusted citations, and incomplete 2026 coverage limit inference. The findings describe research activity, not clinical adoption, safety, effectiveness, or causality.

documents.abstract: Se examinó la gobernanza algorítmica aplicada en la administración tributaria ecuatoriana mediante los sistemas Orión y Falcon, con el objetivo de determinar la compatibilidad del uso de inteligencia artificial y analítica de riesgos con la transparencia administrativa, la protección de datos personales y los derechos del contribuyente, se planteó qué garantías jurídicas debieron regir la selección automatizada de casos y la actuación fiscalizadora posterior, el alcance comprendió normativa constitucional, tributaria, administrativa y de protección de datos, documentos institucionales y estándares internacionales, se aplicó un enfoque jurídico cualitativo, documental, analítico y comparado, complementado con una matriz ordinal de doce dimensiones, seis tablas y seis figuras, los resultados evidenciaron información pública parcial sobre finalidad, seguridad y gestión institucional, junto con vacíos sobre variables, validación, explicabilidad, supervisión y auditoría, se concluyó que la legitimidad exigió intervención humana, trazabilidad, evaluación de impacto, transparencia escalonada, contradicción y revisión independiente, con garantías efectivas de defensa. Palabras clave: auditoría algorítmica, debido proceso, explicabilidad, protección de datos, reserva tributaria Abstract Algorithmic governance in Ecuadorian tax administration through the Orion and Falcon systems was examined within a framework of risk-based digital enforcement and constitutional accountability in public decision-making processes affecting taxpayers, to determine whether artificial intelligence and risk analytics were compatible with administrative transparency, personal data protection, and taxpayer rights, the research question addressed which legal safeguards should have governed automated case selection and subsequent audit action, the scope covered constitutional, tax, administrative, and data protection rules, institutional documents, and international standards, a qualitative, documentary, analytical, and comparative legal approach was applied, supplemented by an ordinal matrix of twelve dimensions, six tables, and six figures, the findings showed partial public information on purpose, security, and institutional management, together with gaps concerning variables, validation, explainability, supervision, and auditing, the analysis concluded that legitimacy required meaningful human intervention, traceability, impact assessment, tiered transparency, challenge procedures, independent review, and effective safeguards for defense. Keywords: algorithmic auditing, data protection, due process, explainability, tax secrecy

In this scholarly dialogue for Media, Technology, and Governance , Guilherme Canela reflects on the centrality of governance in contemporary debates over media, technology, and the global information ecosystem. Drawing on his long-standing work with journalists, governments, civil society, regulators, judges, researchers, and international organizations, Canela situates freedom of expression, access to information, and digital transformation within a broader human rights framework. The conversation begins with Canela's professional trajectory from Latin America to UNESCO headquarters in Paris, then turns to the challenges posed by generative artificial intelligence, platform power, journalism's economic viability, and the need for multistakeholder governance. Canela argues that although technologies change, the principles of journalism, human rights, transparency, accountability, and meaningful participation remain essential. He also calls for scholars to study information and journalism as public goods, the growing attacks on accountability systems, and the ways academic evidence can inform policymaking without sacrificing independence. The dialogue concludes with a message to researchers: governance is the key topic of the coming years, and the academic community is needed to provide the evidence, concepts, and critical debate required to meet that challenge.

Multi-reward reinforcement learning offers a promising framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with diverse objectives, but conflicting reward signals can induce ambiguous update directions and hinder stable optimization. Existing approaches address such conflicts through reward reweighting, gradient coordination, or rollout filtering, yet they primarily operate on per-response or group-level optimization signals and underexploit relational information among sampled responses. As a result, conflict-filtered rollouts may still contain useful supervision that is discarded during training. We propose Group Pareto-Dominance Policy Optimization (GPDPO), a multi-reward policy optimization method that recovers pairwise supervision from conflict-filtered rollouts. GPDPO identifies Pareto-dominance relations among sampled responses and converts them into auxiliary preference signals, which are jointly optimized with the original policy objective. This enables more effective reuse of existing rollouts without additional sampling or reward evaluation. Experiments on API-Bank across multiple model scales and reward configurations show that GPDPO consistently outperforms competitive multi-reward optimization baselines. Further analysis demonstrates that GPDPO reduces both group-relative and pairwise reward conflicts, supporting the effectiveness of exploiting relational supervision for multi-reward alignment. Code will be released.

Clinician-facing artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tools can benefit patient care, but also have potential to cause physical or psychological patient harm. Opinions differ among stakeholders on who should be held responsible when such events occur – the clinician, the developer or vendor, the deploying institution, or some combination. Under current Australian tort law, clinicians remain primarily responsible for patient harm, even if software is shown to be flawed. As a result, clinicians may avoid or delay using AI tools despite demonstrated benefits to patient care. We briefly describe unique legal challenges posed by the use of AI tools, propose a framework for sharing liability among all parties according to their contribution to AI-related harm, and, failing this, offer nine strategies that clinicians and health services can adopt now to lower their liability risk.

documents.abstract: Green and sustainable computing has evolved from a narrow focus on reducing the energy consumed by computer hardware into a broader discipline concerned with energy efficiency, distributed architectures, artificial intelligence, environmental impact, and lifecycle sustainability. This paper presents a structured review and trend analysis based on the findings reported in a recent large-scale study of 11,119 Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 1960 and 2025. The reviewed study used BERTopic with transformer-based embeddings, UMAP dimensionality reduction, HDBSCAN clustering, and temporal analysis to identify 36 research topics. This paper reorganizes those findings into an IJARSCT-style review format and synthesizes the major research directions, thematic groups, developmental stages, challenges, and future opportunities. The evidence shows that virtualization and hardware-efficiency themes have historically been important, while edge computing, AI-supported systems, neuromorphic architectures, UAV computing, and environmentally aware computation have gained research attention. The review also highlights limitations associated with database coverage, metadata quality, topic interpretation, and the use of relative topic prevalence. The resulting framework can help students and researchers understand the changing landscape of green computing and identify areas for further investigation.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that studies intelligent machine learning, including various advanced tools capable of mimicking human intelligence. AI plays an important role in the research field, especially in new drug discovery. AI can tackle many disciplines, including computer science, psychology, and philosophy. AI can work in various fields including science, technology and the pharmaceutical as well as natural science sector to improve efficacy and productivity. AI is now widely used in many industries and research fields because of the high-performance of computer hardware, ample storage, easily available software, and also be a cost effective. In recent years, the continuous advances in Machine learning (ML) algorithms have led to the development of Deep learning (DL) techniques with stronger capabilities in handling big data, which can further assist in identifying natural products and validation of computer-assisted lead identification. This review mainly summarized the rational application and advantages of AI based models to enhance the drug discovery process, including the Natural drug discovery and optimizing drug structures through ML/DL computational tools.

Background Digital repositories and databases facilitate faster dissemination, transparency, and stakeholder collaboration. This review aimed to map and evaluate such digital infrastructures, focusing on their scope, content, functionality, adherence to FAIR (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability and Reuse) principles, and user interface and experiences (UI/UX). Methods A review of global digital health policy repositories was conducted across multiple search engines and databases. The review targeted digital repositories that systematically collate health policy documents at a global level. Two country-specific repositories with a bearing on global health policies were also included. Results The study identified 59 global health policy repositories, with 15 matching our inclusion criteria evaluated in detail. These repositories contain vast amounts of data and are generally freely accessible, rendering them immensely rich sources for health policy documents, though with significant variability in content and coverage. The majority have a health focus, including HIV/AIDS, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH); about a third are broader and more emerging health threats are often neglected. Accessibility and usability are limited, with basic UI features such as search and filtering tools are present for almost all repositories and a notable lack of advanced analytics or artificial intelligence capabilities. Furthermore, many repositories struggle to adhere to FAIR principles, reducing their utility and potential for integration. Sustainability is also a concern, as funding often relies on short-term projects or philanthropic support, undermining long-term viability. Conclusion These issues collectively hinder the ability of digital health policy repositories to support comprehensive and timely global health policy development. To unlock the full potential of existing or new repositories for health policy, identified challenges should be tackled systematically. We provide specific recommendations aimed at driving the development of equitable, inclusive, high-functioning repositories and strengthening evidence-driven global health policy systems.

Heterogeneity is a defining feature of modern data: individuals, subpopulations, sites, modalities, tasks, and time points may differ in distributions, associations, treatment effects, or decision objectives. This review develops a unified perspective in which heterogeneous analysis is a problem of structured information borrowing: deciding what should be shared, what should remain distinct, and how uncertainty about that structure should enter inference and decisions. We connect classical stratification, interaction models, finite mixtures, mixed-effects models, and empirical Bayes with subgroup discovery, individualized learning, synthetic data generation, large language models, federated learning, privacy, security, and mobile health. Precision medicine provides a central example: subgroup rules offer interpretable approximations to individualized response surfaces, whereas partially pooled models stabilize patient-specific estimation. Across applications, the same tensions recur: population averages can conceal consequential variation, unrestricted personalization is unstable, adaptive subgroup discovery creates selection bias, and borrowing across incompatible sources causes negative transfer. These difficulties are amplified in contemporary AI, where sparse user histories, entangled representations, heterogeneous preferences, feedback loops, distribution shift, and privacy constraints make reliable personalization and evaluation especially challenging. We conclude with an agenda for calibrated personalization that integrates multilevel representations, selective borrowing, subgroup-aware evaluation, and valid uncertainty quantification.

Higher education is confronting its fourth major disruption within a single career arc, one defined not by a single policy shift or budget crisis but by a deep cultural reckoning. Over the past 30 years, 3 technological revolutions, the Internet, the smartphone, and generative artificial intelligence (AI), have systematically collapsed distance, time, and trust. Rather than transform in response, higher education layered new technologies atop legacy structures, raising costs and eroding public credibility. Today, the sector faces a collapse of legitimacy, fueling political interventions and public skepticism. This chapter argues that surviving and leading through this era requires more than strategic planning or operational efficiency. It demands a posture of resilient, continual crisis leadership grounded in human connection. Drawing from decades of leadership experience across multiple institutions and crises, Timothy Chester offers six practical strategies designed to rebuild trust and guide institutions through ongoing volatility. In an age where disruption is a permanent condition, this chapter serves as both a warning and a field guide, calling leaders to embrace clarity, compassion, and steady presence as higher education navigates its most profound test yet.

Graceful degradation is a key mechanism employed by large-scale systems to handle overload conditions. Its importance has grown further as GPU-intensive LLM inference introduces persistent capacity constraints that cannot be addressed through provisioning alone. Common degradation approaches rely on service-level mechanisms such as load shedding and circuit breakers, or on feature-level switches (some manually controlled) to preserve availability and quality. While effective at protecting services, such approaches lead to untestable product states and thereby unpredictable product quality. We present HiLO (High Load Optimizer), an automated product-level degradation system designed to handle graceful degradation at scale. HiLO maps observed load to a product state lattice: a small set of pre-validated product states, partially ordered by degradation severity. Dependencies are resolved at design time enabling deterministic and continuous control without requiring runtime dependency discovery. The same abstraction applies unchanged across heterogeneous services, including GPU-intensive deep models, LLMs and their serving layers. At Microsoft, HiLO is deployed in Bing (serving over a billion monthly active users), where it manages on average two traffic surges per week across all datacenters, bounding OneDCG (relevance) drop to under 0.5 points (the operational target) even under sustained load exceeding 2$\times$ baseline peak. HiLO complements existing service-level protections with product-level coordination and makes product quality measurable, testable and predictable.

AI applications, including virtual patients and conversational agents, offer promising enhancements to communication skills training for pharmacy students, providing interactive and repetitive practice opportunities that traditional methods may lack.
